cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Puerto Rico
cases.FraudEntity: Josué Saez Rodríguez (seller/distributor of unauthorized drug products); Chancey Irmaries Olmed Pérez (seller/distributor of unauthorized drug products); Carlos Andrés Rendón Bermúdez (performed dental procedures without a dental license); Jandiel Santos Rodríguez (Rendón Bermúdez's Puerto Rico representative/appointment coordinator)
cases.State_County: Puerto Rico - Comerío; Puerto Rico - San Lorenzo; Ohio - Franklin County (Columbus)
cases.SchemeSummary: Two separate indictments in Puerto Rico: Saez Rodríguez and Olmed Pérez allegedly advertised, sold and distributed drug products they were not authorized to possess or distribute (Semaglutide, Mounjaro, Tirzepatide and steroids), charged with wire fraud conspiracy and drug misbranding; separately, Rendón Bermúdez allegedly performed dental work (braces, whitening, cleanings, veneers, cavity work, tooth grinding, anesthesia, antibiotic prescriptions) without a dental license while Santos Rodríguez advertised the services on social media, booked appointments and falsely represented him as a licensed dentist.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
cases.FraudEntity: International Union of Journeymen and Allied Trades (IUJAT) (labor union); United Service Workers Union, IUJAT National Union (USWU) (labor union); Home Healthcare Workers of America, IUJAT (HHWA) (labor union); Service Professionals Union Local 726 IUJAT (LOCAL 726) (labor union); United Welfare Fund - Welfare Division (UWF) (employee benefit plan)
cases.PayerName: U.S. Small Business Administration (Paycheck Protection Program)
cases.SchemeSummary: Between April 16 and April 20, 2020, four labor unions and an affiliated employee welfare benefit plan each submitted PPP loan applications falsely certifying eligibility under SBA rules, though as 501(c)(5) non-profits they were ineligible; they received $3,316,966 in total and obtained full loan forgiveness, despite prior warnings from an SBA regional employee and the AFL-CIO that unions were not eligible. The defendants collectively agreed to pay $3,850,000 to resolve False Claims Act allegations arising from a sealed qui tam suit joined by the government.

cases.State_County: California - Los Angeles County (Los Angeles, Artesia, Glendale, Tarzana, Chatsworth, Covina, Carson, Torrance, El Segundo, Long Beach, Lakewood); California - Orange County (Anaheim, Huntington Beach); California - Ventura County (Simi Valley); Idaho - Coeur d'Alene
cases.PayerName: Medicare; International Longshore and Warehouse Union Pacific Maritime Association (ILWU-PMA) health plan; other private health insurers
cases.SchemeSummary: Coordinated takedown of eight defendants across several related schemes totaling more than $50 million in intended losses: hospice operators (Minerd, $9.17M billed/$8.51M paid; the Gills, $5.2M billed/$4M paid; Palma and Catbagan, $4.8M billed/$4.2M paid; Tindimubona, $3.8M billed/$3.4M paid; Lauritzen, $580K billed/$526K paid) enrolled Medicare beneficiaries who were not terminally ill, paid cash kickbacks to beneficiaries and marketers for referrals, billed for services never provided or not medically necessary, used a nominee owner to hide an excluded operator, and forged a physician signature on Medicare enrollment forms; separately, chiropractic/physical-therapy defendants billed the ILWU-PMA union health plan and other private insurers for unneeded or non-existent services using fake chart notes and other providers' names and IDs to evade terminations (Aulava-Moala group $19M; Cartmell/Surace $9.14M billed/$6.43M paid; Griffen $4.9M billed/$2.5M paid), plus a defendant who fabricated immigration medical exam forms posing as a nurse or doctor.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Kentucky
cases.FraudEntity: Addiction Recovery Care, LLC (drug rehabilitation provider); Pioneer Health Group, LLC (affiliate); Science Hill Family Care, LLC (affiliate)
cases.SchemeSummary: ARC and affiliates allegedly billed Kentucky Medicaid for behavioral health services (psychotherapy, psychiatric evaluations, mental health assessments) delivered by lower-level workers but coded as if furnished by higher-licensed clinicians, and billed group therapy as higher-paying individual therapy; affiliates also billed duplicate office visits, visits already covered by an inclusive per diem rate, and care management services by uncredentialed staff. Resolved by a $16,205,774.05 civil judgment following a 2023 qui tam suit by employees.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
cases.FraudEntity: Yolanda Matthews (owner of adult day care center)
cases.SchemeSummary: Owner of an adult day care center billed Medicare over $539,000 for psychotherapy services never provided, including claims for beneficiaries who were hospitalized elsewhere or already deceased, and forged claims in the names of social workers no longer employed there.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
cases.FraudEntity: Tony King (operator of Agape Love Adult Day Care LLC); Agape Love Adult Day Care LLC
cases.PayerName: Missouri Medicaid (Adult Day Care Waiver program)
cases.SchemeSummary: King allegedly billed Missouri Medicaid's Adult Day Care Waiver program for 10 hours of daily care when Agape Love Adult Day Care provided only about half that, and submitted claims for day care services for patients who were absent or hospitalized, totaling $1.47 million in false claims.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Georgia
cases.FraudEntity: Jitesh Patel, M.D. (physician/owner); Advanced Urology, Inc. and affiliated companies
cases.PayerName: Medicare; Georgia Medicaid; TRICARE; Department of Veterans Affairs
cases.SchemeSummary: Whistleblowers alleged the urology practice maximized revenue by performing and billing federal health care programs for medically unnecessary procedures - permanent sacral nerve stimulator implants without trial testing, cystoscopy/retrograde pyelograms, electromyography on nearly every new patient, and thousands of ultrasounds - and by billing for Direct Visual Internal Urethrotomy procedures that were never performed when only a simpler urethral dilation was done. Settled for $14 million, of which relators receive $2,940,000.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
cases.FraudEntity: Aetna Inc. (Medicare Advantage Organization / national insurer)
cases.SchemeSummary: Aetna allegedly used a one-sided 'chart review' program for payment year 2015 to add unsupported risk-adjustment diagnosis codes to CMS for Medicare Advantage enrollees while declining to delete codes its own reviews failed to substantiate ($106.2M), and for payment years 2018-2023 submitted or failed to delete morbid-obesity diagnosis codes for beneficiaries whose recorded BMI did not support that diagnosis ($11.5M), inflating capitated risk-adjusted payments; resolved via a $117.7M FCA settlement including a $2,012,500 whistleblower share.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice — Civil Division; U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
cases.FraudEntity: Aetna Inc. (Medicare Advantage Organization / national insurer)
cases.SchemeSummary: Aetna allegedly submitted and failed to withdraw inaccurate, unsupported diagnosis codes for Medicare Advantage enrollees to inflate CMS risk-adjustment capitation payments: for payment year 2015 it used chart-review results only to add revenue-generating codes while ignoring chart reviews that failed to substantiate previously submitted codes (which would have required repayment), and for payment years 2018-2023 it submitted or retained morbid-obesity diagnosis codes for beneficiaries whose recorded BMI did not support the diagnosis, while falsely certifying the data's accuracy. Resolved via $117.7 million settlement, including a qui tam suit whose relator receives $2,012,500.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division and U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Pennsylvania
cases.FraudEntity: Ahold Delhaize USA Inc. (supermarket chain operator of in-store retail pharmacies, including Giant, Hannaford, Stop & Shop, and Food Lion)
cases.PayerName: Medicare Part D; Medicaid (federal and participating state programs); TRICARE
cases.FraudType: Inflated usual and customary price reporting
FraudTypeAll: Inflated usual and customary price reporting
cases.SchemeSummary: Ahold Delhaize's in-store pharmacies ran prescription savings programs giving enrolled members discounted drug prices, but allegedly did not report those discounted prices as their 'usual and customary' prices on claims to Medicare Part D, Medicaid and TRICARE; because U&C prices act as ceiling prices in the payment formulas, the programs paid inflated amounts. Resolved for $40 million ($32.9 million federal share) following a pharmacist's qui tam suit, with the relator receiving $6,083,587.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: Tommie Robinson (Alabama-based doctor)
cases.SchemeSummary: Robinson signed pre-populated doctors' orders generated from telemarketing calls to Medicare beneficiaries, without contacting them or establishing a provider-patient relationship; DME suppliers and genetic testing laboratories then used those signed orders to submit over $2.7 million in medically unnecessary claims to Medicare.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Tennessee
cases.FraudEntity: American Health Companies, LLC, dba American Health Partners (nursing home owner/operator); Lewis County Nursing and Rehabilitation, LLC, dba AHC Lewis County (131-bed nursing facility subsidiary)
cases.SchemeSummary: AHC Lewis County allegedly billed Medicare and TennCare for nursing home services that were grossly substandard or worthless - failing to provide proper wound care, infection control, fall protection, and prevention of weight loss and loss of range of motion, and overprescribing antipsychotics - while collecting full payment; AHP agreed to pay $2,090,309 ($1,196,074 federal, $894,235 to Tennessee).

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: ASD Specialty Healthcare, LLC d/b/a Oncology Supply Company (specialty pharmaceutical distributor, subsidiary of Cencora, Inc., f/k/a AmerisourceBergen Corporation); International Oncology Network (ION) (Cencora subsidiary)
cases.SchemeSummary: ASD/Oncology Supply and affiliate ION provided health care providers and medical practice executives with meals and alcohol at high-end restaurants, golf rounds, and outings at bars and nightclubs (sometimes covering spouses' expenses), at Large Practice Program conferences and outside them, to induce purchases of specialty pharmaceutical products; the government alleged this caused physicians to submit kickback-tainted claims to Medicare and Medicaid. Resolved for $1 million under the False Claims Act following a qui tam suit, with the relator receiving 17.5%.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
cases.FraudEntity: Timothy Bogen (Amtrak employee); Quinton Johnson (Amtrak employee); Gregory Richardson (Amtrak employee); Dion Jacob (Amtrak employee); Kevin Frink (Amtrak employee); Michael Toal (Amtrak employee); David McBrien (Amtrak employee); Damany Walker (Amtrak employee); David Lonergan (Amtrak employee); Rodolfo Rivera (Amtrak employee); Punson Figueroa (acupuncturist); Michael DeNicola (podiatrist)
cases.SchemeSummary: Ten Amtrak employees accepted thousands of dollars in cash kickbacks from health care providers (including an acupuncturist and a podiatrist) in exchange for allowing their Amtrak employee health insurance plan to be billed for services that were never rendered and were not medically necessary; the plan paid over $11 million in fraudulent claims tied to the providers. Figures span multiple defendants; four employees received two years' probation, and provider Punson Figueroa was sentenced to 34 months in prison, with other sentencings pending.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division and U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Alaska
cases.FraudEntity: Dr. Claribel Tan (rheumatologist, clinic owner); Daniel Tan (office manager, husband)
cases.PayerName: More than 10 health insurance plans (not individually named)
cases.SchemeSummary: Over 15 years the Tans billed insurance plans for 4,829 units of injectable rheumatology medications while purchasing only 369 units, secretly injecting patients with free samples, expired drugs or substitute medications, and also billed for office visits of exaggerated length and services never provided; they then overstated clinic expenses on 2014, 2015 and 2017 tax returns and failed to file returns for 2018-2021, costing the IRS over $4.2 million. Claribel Tan received 78 months; Daniel Tan received 3 years' probation with 2 years home confinement, and figures (including $10.4M forfeited, $6.3M paid toward restitution and $1.8M FCA civil settlement) span both defendants.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Alaska
cases.FraudEntity: Dr. Claribel Tan (rheumatologist, clinic owner); Daniel Tan (husband, clinic office/management worker)
cases.PayerName: TRICARE; more than 10 other health insurance plans
cases.SchemeSummary: At their Anchorage rheumatology clinic the Tans billed TRICARE and more than 10 insurance plans for 4,829 units of injectable biologic medications while purchasing only 369 units, secretly underdosing patients, substituting free samples, expired drugs, or medication bought for other patients; they also billed for longer office visits and services never provided, and overstated clinic drug expenses on 2014, 2015 and 2017 tax returns while failing to file 2018-2021 returns, causing a $4.2 million IRS loss. Figures cover both defendants: Dr. Tan received 78 months in prison, Daniel Tan three years' probation, and together they forfeited $10.4 million in seized proceeds, paid $6.3 million toward restitution and $1.8 million to settle False Claims Act civil claims.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division (National Fraud Enforcement Division/Fraud Section); U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey
cases.FraudEntity: Michael Emma (member of the '10th and O Crew'); Michael Procopio (crew leader); Frank Procopio (crew leader)
cases.SchemeSummary: Emma obtained prescription oxycodone pills from area doctors' offices and, with co-conspirators of South Philadelphia's '10th and O Crew,' sold them in shifts out of a 24-hour restaurant; law enforcement made a controlled buy from a co-conspirator who was then observed counting the proceeds with Emma. Emma received 60 months; co-conspirator leaders Michael and Frank Procopio received 72 months and 57 months respectively.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Wisconsin
cases.FraudEntity: Apple Medical Clinic; Dr. Michael Johnson (principal, and national distributor of the RST Sanexas device)
cases.SchemeSummary: Clinic and its physician billed Medicare for electrical muscle stimulation using the RST Sanexas neoGEN device combined with vitamin blend injections and ancillary services such as epidermal nerve fiber density testing that were not medically reasonable or necessary and excluded from Medicare coverage under NCD 160.7.1; the doctor also marketed the device for indications outside its FDA clearance and advertised the treatments as Medicare-billable. Settlement of $382,362.95 (based on ability to pay) comprises a $175,000 payment plus CMS retention of $207,362.95.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
cases.FraudEntity: Marisol Rodriguez, also known as Marisol Colon (Advanced Practice Registered Nurse)
cases.SchemeSummary: An APRN allegedly submitted more than 15,000 Connecticut Medicaid claims totaling over $1.35 million for medication management services never provided - including for patients who had stopped seeing her months or years earlier, patients who were hospitalized, incarcerated or deceased, and for periods when she was working full-time elsewhere or collecting unemployment; her billings ranked first among a peer group of 116 APRNs.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division, Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Arizona
cases.FraudEntity: Tri-City Cardiology, P.C. (physician group); Dr. Jaskamal Kahlon (physician); Dr. Joshua D. Cohen (physician); Dr. M. Joshua Berkowitz (physician)
cases.SchemeSummary: The cardiology group and three physicians allegedly billed federal health programs for medically unnecessary ablations of perforator veins that did not meet accepted treatment criteria, and knowingly mismeasured or misdocumented reflux duration, vein diameter, patient symptoms and conservative therapy in medical records to make the procedures appear justified; resolved for $4.75 million across all defendants.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division, Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section
cases.FraudEntity: Southwest Orthopedic and Spine Hospital LLC d/b/a OASIS Hospital (surgical hospital); United Surgical Partners International Inc. (USPI); Dignity/USP Phoenix Surgery Centers LLC
cases.SchemeSummary: OASIS Hospital allegedly made improper financial contributions - in the form of interest payments on convertible bonds issued to Southwest Orthopedic and Spine Hospital Physicians Group - to a physician group that referred patients to the hospital, and then billed federal health care programs for the referred services in violation of the Anti-Kickback Statute and Stark Law. USPI disclosed the arrangements after a 2019 internal compliance review; the $5.6 million settlement covers all three entities.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division, and U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Arkansas (U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Arkansas); U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Pennsylvania
cases.FraudEntity: Advanced Pathology Solutions PLLC (formerly Advanced Pathology Solutions LLC) (anatomic pathology laboratory); APS MSO LLC (management services organization); Kevin Hannah (owner/CEO); Donell Burkett (current or former owner); Daniel Hunter Pledger (current or former owner)
cases.SchemeSummary: APS set up and managed 'lean labs' inside gastroenterology practices nationwide, letting the practices bill for preparing and staining biopsy slides in exchange for exclusively referring slides to APS's North Little Rock lab for pathologist interpretation - alleged kickbacks under the AKS/FCA; APS also directed lean lab staff to automatically order 'special stains' before a pathologist reviewed the routine H&E stain, plus additional 'confirmatory' immunohistochemical tests, generating medically unnecessary claims to Medicare and Medicaid. The settlement also resolves allegations that APS and CEO Kevin Hannah paid Richard Sorgnard 4% volume-based commissions (Nov. 2018-Nov. 2020) to induce referrals for epidermal nerve fiber density testing. The $30 million is a total across APS entities and the three owners.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Tennessee
cases.FraudEntity: Heather May Wilbanks Greene (unlicensed individual posing as a registered nurse)
cases.SchemeSummary: Greene allegedly used the stolen license numbers of two licensed Tennessee registered nurses and submitted false resumes misrepresenting her education, experience and licensure to obtain nursing jobs at more than 30 health care facilities, including nursing homes and correctional institutions, despite never attending nursing school or passing the NCLEX-RN; she performed licensed-nurse duties such as administering medications and evaluating patients and collected $200,000 in wages to which she was not entitled.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Texas
cases.FraudEntity: Hambardzum Minasyan (developer/administrator of RedLine infostealer infrastructure); Maxim Rudometov (alleged co-conspirator, developer/administrator)
cases.SchemeSummary: Non-healthcare cybercrime case: defendant allegedly helped develop and administer the RedLine infostealer malware, registering virtual private servers, internet domains and file-sharing repositories to host and distribute the malware to paying affiliates, collecting affiliate payments via a cryptocurrency account registered in November 2021, and laundering cybercrime proceeds through cryptocurrency exchanges; the malware stole victims' data including access devices and financial information.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Georgia
cases.FraudEntity: Arthritis & Rheumatology Center, P.C. (medical practice); Jatin Patel, M.D. (owner)
cases.SchemeSummary: ARC allegedly used unlicensed medical assistants to administer chemotherapy infusions to patients in violation of Georgia law, then billed Medicare for those infusion services, which Medicare does not pay for when rendered in violation of state law; resolved via a $2.18 million FCA settlement from a qui tam suit, with the relator receiving $414,200.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: Nova Psychiatric Services, P.C. (behavioral health clinic); Patriot Eldercare, Inc. (behavioral health clinic); Alexandra Accardi, M.D. (psychiatrist, founder/owner, president and director); Miguel Saravia (Chief Operating Officer of Nova)
cases.PayerName: Medicare; Massachusetts Medicaid; Massachusetts Group Insurance Commission (GIC)
cases.SchemeSummary: Nova and Patriot billed Medicare, Medicaid and the Massachusetts GIC for psychotherapy and medication management services that their behavioral health clinicians never performed; the COO directed untrained independent contractors outside the billing department to alter claims before submission by adding extra psychotherapy and medication management billing codes, despite employee complaints. The companies and owner Accardi paid $1.4 million to resolve False Claims Act allegations (qui tam, relator gets 17.5%), while COO Saravia pleaded guilty to six healthcare fraud counts and was sentenced to 3.5 months in prison with $561,141 restitution.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Georgia
cases.FraudEntity: Mira Stallings (licensed behavioral therapist, owner of ABAscape LLC); ABAscape LLC
cases.SchemeSummary: Owner of a behavioral therapy agency billed TRICARE more than $652,000 for individual and group therapy services for developmentally disabled patients that were never provided or not provided as billed, receiving over $572,000; she also obtained nearly $1 million in CARES Act EIDL funds certified for working capital and spent them on personal debts, family salary payments and a dog-breeding compound.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division (Fraud Section) and U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Maryland
cases.FraudEntity: Nader Pourhassan (Chief Executive Officer of CytoDyn); CytoDyn (publicly traded biotech company)
cases.State_County: Washington - Vancouver (CytoDyn headquarters); Oregon - Lake Oswego (defendant's residence)
cases.SchemeSummary: The CEO of CytoDyn made false public announcements to investors about the prospects of FDA approval for an investigational HIV/COVID-19 drug, artificially inflating the company's stock price, then sold his 4.8 million personal shares at the inflated prices for $4.4 million. Convicted at trial in December 2024 of securities fraud, wire fraud and insider trading; sentenced to 30 months and ordered to pay over $5.3 million restitution plus over $4.4 million forfeiture.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
cases.FraudEntity: Armen Muradyan (owner/operator of Genex Laboratories Inc.); Genex Laboratories Inc. (Burbank blood-testing laboratory)
cases.PayerName: Medicare; U.S. Small Business Administration (COVID-19 EIDL program)
cases.SchemeSummary: Muradyan, barred by Medicare from submitting claims, paid a long-time friend ('L.S.') $2,000 per month to pose as owner of his Burbank blood-testing lab Genex Laboratories, submit the Medicare enrollment paperwork, and hold bank accounts that Muradyan controlled, so that millions in Medicare blood-test reimbursements were wired to nominee accounts and spent on his mortgage, gambling and personal expenses; he further had the nominee report Genex's income on the nominee's personal returns, evading about $11.2 million in taxes on $23.9 million of unreported income, and obtained a $99,900 SBA EIDL loan by falsely claiming an entity called GenMed had employees and $800,000 in 2019 income.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
cases.FraudEntity: Shawn Tyson (Licensed Alcohol and Drug Abuse Counselor); Thelma "Wendy" Epps (suspended Medicaid provider); Dennis Tomczak (licensed counselor)
cases.SchemeSummary: Tyson, a licensed drug and alcohol counselor, billed Connecticut Medicaid for psychotherapy counseling sessions that were never provided, and also billed under his own provider number for services purportedly rendered by Epps, who had been suspended from Medicaid, falsely representing that he personally performed them; he submitted fraudulent patient records during a Medicaid audit to conceal the scheme. Restitution of $670,960.72 is owed in part jointly and severally with Epps and counselor Dennis Tomczak.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Tennessee
cases.FraudEntity: Helen Boerman (optometric physician, owner of Brentwood Eye Care); Brentwood Eye Care
cases.PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid (TennCare, Tennessee); Federal Employees Health Benefits Program
cases.SchemeSummary: Optometric physician billed Medicare through her practice for new single-use wound care products she had not purchased or used, splitting single-use products across patients, and billed for wound care product placements on dates when patients had no appointments; she directed staff to create false records to support the fabricated service dates. She admitted submitting roughly $11 million in false Medicare claims and receiving about $6.9 million, and also submitted false claims to TennCare and FEHB.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section (Health Care Fraud Unit)
cases.FraudEntity: Renat Abramov (former bank relationship manager, Sheepshead Bay branch); transnational criminal organization (unnamed co-conspirators posing as owners of fake medical equipment companies)
cases.SchemeSummary: A transnational criminal organization allegedly submitted more than $10 billion in fraudulent Medicare claims through sham durable medical equipment companies using identities stolen from over one million Americans; Abramov, a bank relationship manager, opened accounts for straw owners using fake corporate registration documents so the Medicare and insurer checks could be deposited and then moved offshore and into cryptocurrency, laundering more than $8 million.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Michigan
cases.FraudEntity: Rabih Hamdan (business owner/pharmacy owner)
cases.PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan
cases.SchemeSummary: Pharmacy owner submitted false claims to Medicare, Medicaid and Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan for prescription drugs that were medically unnecessary or never dispensed; in many cases the pharmacy lacked inventory to dispense the billed drugs and no physician had ordered the medications. Total false claims of at least $1.9 million over five years, with proceeds used for personal benefit.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Idaho
cases.FraudEntity: Niki Rashel Cook (purported registered nurse/licensed practical nurse)
cases.State_County: Idaho - Caldwell (Canyon County); Boise area healthcare facilities
cases.SchemeSummary: Cook was indicted for wire fraud and aggravated identity theft for using other people's names and nursing licenses to falsely present herself as a registered nurse and licensed practical nurse, obtaining nursing jobs at a behavioral health hospital, a rehabilitation hospital, a skilled nursing facility, and hospice businesses, and earning over $22,000 in wages she was not qualified to receive.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division Fraud Section; U.S. District Court for the Central District of California
cases.FraudEntity: Violetta Mailyan (doctor, owner/operator of Healthy Way Medical Center)
cases.SchemeSummary: Mailyan, through her cosmetic clinic, billed Medicare roughly $45 million for thousands of Botox injections purportedly treating chronic migraines that were never provided (including on days her clinic was closed, while she was on vacation abroad, and for a beneficiary who was incarcerated) or were purely cosmetic/without referral; she backdated claims and fabricated patient records and consent forms, then altered records given to federal agents in response to a grand jury subpoena. Jury found a Tesla Model X, Cybertruck, $251,124 in bank funds, $7,312,037 in brokerage accounts and four properties with $7,343,636 equity forfeitable as proceeds.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Minnesota
cases.FraudEntity: Karan Gupta (senior director of data analytics, Optum, Inc.)
cases.State_County: Minnesota - Hennepin County (Minneapolis); California; New Jersey
cases.PayerName: Optum, Inc. (UnitedHealth Group subsidiary - employer, not a claims payer)
cases.SchemeSummary: Gupta, a senior director at Optum, gave a lifelong friend a false resume and hired him into a managerial data engineering job he was unqualified for; for nearly four years the friend performed no work while drawing a salary above $100,000 with raises and bonuses, and kicked back more than half of it to Gupta, who concealed the payments through cash deposits at a New Jersey bank branch and later by using a debit card tied to the friend's direct-deposit account to withdraw funds from California ATMs. Gupta's frauds against Optum totaled more than $1.2 million.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
cases.FraudEntity: Paul Randall (scheme organizer/marketer); Kyrollos Mekail (pharmacist and owner of Monte Vista Pharmacy); Patricia Anderson (nurse practitioner); Monte Vista Pharmacy
cases.State_County: California - Orange County (Orange); California - Riverside County (Moreno Valley); California - Los Angeles County (West Hills)
cases.SchemeSummary: Exploiting Medi-Cal's temporary suspension of prior-authorization at the start of 2022, Randall used Mekail's Monte Vista Pharmacy to bill tens of millions per month for high-reimbursement generic drugs (e.g., pain creams, Folite tablets, meloxicam billed at ~$13,424 per prescription) compounded in unique dosages/package quantities that fell outside Medi-Cal maximum price caps; Randall paid kickbacks to marketers for beneficiary information and to nurse practitioner Anderson to sign pre-filled prescriptions without ever seeing patients, and drugs were often never dispensed. Randall took roughly 40% of the pharmacy's profit and laundered proceeds through a third party to pay Anderson. $269,120,829 billed and about $178,746,556 paid; co-defendants Mekail and Anderson also pleaded guilty and await sentencing.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
cases.FraudEntity: Louis Morelli (psychiatrist, owner of psychiatry practice in Smithville, New Jersey)
cases.State_County: New Jersey - Cape May County; New Jersey - Smithville (Atlantic County)
cases.SchemeSummary: Psychiatrist issued invalid prescriptions for Adderall, Vyvanse, and Xanax to 17 patients outside the usual course of professional practice and without legitimate medical purpose, sometimes in exchange for sexual activity, images or videos, and to known addicts and suspected diverters; the prescriptions were intended to defraud and mislead dispensing pharmacies and the insurers, government benefit programs, and other third parties that paid for the drugs.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of New York
cases.FraudEntity: Joseph Carl (operator of Carl's Cab); Randolph Ekstrom a/k/a 'Randy' (operator/associate of Carl's Cab); Carl's Cab (Medicaid-enrolled transportation provider)
cases.State_County: New York - Saratoga County; New York - Rensselaer County
cases.PayerName: Medicaid (New York State Department of Health)
cases.SchemeSummary: Operators of Carl's Cab, a Medicaid-enrolled non-emergency medical transportation provider, allegedly billed New York Medicaid for 'ghost rides' and trips where recipients were never transported or never seen by a provider, and inflated reimbursement by billing group transports as multiple individual trips; they also allegedly paid cash and controlled substances to Medicaid recipients to induce them to use Carl's Cab, receiving at least $4,296,374.02 in Medicaid funds.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Tennessee
cases.FraudEntity: Thomas K. Weir (majority owner, Oakley Pharmacy dba Dale Hollow Pharmacy and Clay County Xpress Pharmacy); William L. Donaldson (former owner and pharmacist, Dale Hollow Pharmacy); Pamela Spivey (co-owner, Xpress Pharmacy); Charles Robert 'Bobby' Oakley (minority owner, Dale Hollow Pharmacy); John Polston (pharmacist-in-charge); Michael Griffith (pharmacist-in-charge); Oakley Pharmacy dba Dale Hollow Pharmacy and Clay County Xpress Pharmacy
cases.SchemeSummary: Owners and pharmacists of two Celina, TN pharmacies dispensed controlled substances despite red flags of abuse and diversion (patients traveling long distances in groups, prescriptions without legitimate medical purpose) and billed Medicare Part D and TennCare for those drugs, including medically unnecessary combinations of highly abused drugs; to boost prescription volume they paid patient co-pays, gave patients cash, and issued fictitious 'Monkey Bucks' currency redeemable for cash. Weir received 24 months, $1,419,974 restitution, forfeiture of the pharmacy building/warehouse and a money judgment exceeding $700,000; co-defendant Donaldson got 24 months, while Oakley and Spivey received probation with restitution.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section / National Fraud Enforcement Division
cases.FraudEntity: Heriberto Rivera (CEO of Family Integrative Medicine of Orlando, LLC); Laurent Cassagnol (Advanced Medical Support Assistant, VA Community Care Program); Family Integrative Medicine of Orlando, LLC (FIMO)
cases.PayerName: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs - VA Community Care Program
cases.SchemeSummary: FIMO's CEO paid kickbacks and bribes to a VA Community Care Program medical support assistant to steer VA patients to FIMO for acupuncture, chiropractic and other holistic services; over $14 million in resulting claims were billed to the VA/VACCP, of which more than $11 million was paid.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of California
cases.FraudEntity: Simon Katz; Veronica Katz (former CEO of HealthNow Home Healthcare); Vennesa Herrera (former employee); Pharadja Andrews (former employee); HealthNow Home Healthcare (home health agency)
cases.SchemeSummary: HealthNow Home Healthcare billed Medicare for home health services never provided and for care delivered by unqualified medical professionals acting outside their authorized scope of practice, while altering medical records and forging physician signatures and submitting false documents to California Department of Public Health inspectors to keep its Medicare billing privileges; the agency collected over $3 million and Simon Katz received $300,000, and he instructed a former employee to lie to the FBI. Co-defendant Veronica Katz was sentenced to 24 months with $543,634.34 restitution and a $50,000 fine; Simon Katz was convicted at trial and awaits sentencing.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division (Health and Safety Unit) and U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
cases.FraudEntity: Bryce Cleveland (President and CEO of Scalpa, Inc.); Scalpa, Inc.
cases.SchemeSummary: Cleveland marketed and sold to consumers unapproved and misbranded injectable devices and drugs (ScalpaJECT Hyaluronic Acid, Hyaluron Pen, and the botulinum toxin product 'Scalpatox') through his company Scalpa, Inc., falsely representing that the devices were not subject to FDA regulation; he pleaded guilty to mail fraud, introducing an adulterated device into interstate commerce, and introducing an unapproved new drug into interstate commerce, agreeing to a 4-8 year prison term, restitution, and $800,000 forfeiture.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: Aditya Humad (Chief Financial Officer, SpineFrontier, Inc.); SpineFrontier, Inc. (spinal implant company); Dr. Kingsley R. Chin (Founder, President and CEO); Jason Montone, D.O. (surgeon); John Balzer (medical device distributor)
cases.SchemeSummary: SpineFrontier's CFO and CEO paid surgeons over $540,000 in sham 'consulting' fees ($250-$1,000 per hour) under contracts purportedly for gathering technical product feedback, when in fact the payments induced the surgeons to implant SpineFrontier spinal devices in surgeries reimbursed by Medicare, Medicaid and the Veterans Health Administration, generating millions in company revenue. Settlement figures combine Humad's $150,000+ civil settlement and Chin's $9,500 fine, $40,000 personal and $855,000 company civil settlement payments.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: Aditya Humad (Chief Financial Officer, SpineFrontier, Inc.); Dr. Kingsley R. Chin (Founder, President and CEO, SpineFrontier, Inc.); SpineFrontier, Inc. (spinal implant company); Jason Montone, D.O. (surgeon); John Balzer (medical device distributor); Dr. F. Paul DeGenova; Dr. Michael Murray; Dr. Joseph Shehadi; Dr. Agha Khan; Dr. John Atwater; Dr. John Carlson
cases.SchemeSummary: SpineFrontier's CFO conspired with the company to enter sham consulting contracts with spine surgeons, paying them $250-$1,000 per hour (over $540,000 total) purportedly for product feedback but in reality to induce them to implant SpineFrontier devices in surgeries billed to Medicare, Medicaid and the VA; surgeons did little or no actual consulting work. Figures span multiple defendants: Humad received four months in prison plus a $9,500 fine and a civil settlement of over $150,000; CEO Chin received home confinement, a $9,500 fine, $40,000 personally and $855,000 from his company; six surgeons paid civil FCA settlements totaling roughly $3.3 million.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of South Carolina
cases.FraudEntity: Kevin Dion Hollinshead (Charleston County School District Trustee / board member)
cases.SchemeSummary: Indictment alleges a school board trustee accepted a kickback from a consultant's fee, paid by a construction company he steered to hire the consultant, in exchange for using his official position to influence a failed-bid appeal; separately he allegedly submitted two SBA pandemic relief loan applications in 2020-2021 with false revenue and employee figures and spent proceeds on personal expenses including a medical procedure at a clinic in Mexico. No health care payer was involved.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of North Carolina
cases.FraudEntity: Ronnie Lorenzo Robinson, Jr. (beneficial owner of The Fisher of Men Project, LLC); The Fisher of Men Project, LLC
cases.SchemeSummary: Robinson allegedly obtained personal identifying information of medical professionals and Medicaid recipients and used it to submit approximately $735,000 in claims to North Carolina Medicaid for psychotherapy services that were never provided, receiving about $440,000 in payments; he also allegedly concealed his ownership of the billing company because he had previously been excluded from Medicaid, holding out another person as owner.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
cases.FraudEntity: Michele Rene Muzyka (Advanced Practice Registered Nurse)
cases.SchemeSummary: An APRN prescribed Schedule II and IV amphetamines and benzodiazepines to patients with no legitimate medical need, skipping medical examinations and charging $200 cash per office visit, including to an undercover agent posing as a Medicaid beneficiary; Medicaid paid $287.58 for the unlawful prescriptions written for the undercover agent.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
cases.FraudEntity: Michele Rene Muzyka (Advanced Practice Registered Nurse, APRN)
cases.State_County: Connecticut - New Haven County (Cheshire); Connecticut - Hartford County (New Britain); Connecticut - Middlesex County (Middletown)
cases.SchemeSummary: An APRN enrolled as a Medicare/Medicaid provider prescribed high-dose amphetamines (Adderall) and benzodiazepines (Xanax/alprazolam) to patients with no legitimate medical need, conducting no medical examinations and charging $200 cash per office visit, including to an undercover agent posing as a Medicaid beneficiary; Medicaid paid $287.58 for the unlawful prescriptions written for that agent. Five of her patients died of overdoses between February 2020 and June 2023.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: Sanja Ilic (Chief Regulatory Officer of ExThera Medical Corporation); ExThera Medical Corporation (medical device manufacturer)
cases.State_County: California (ExThera, Northern California; Ilic of Carlsbad); treatments at a clinic in Antigua
cases.FraudType: Concealment of adverse events from FDA
FraudTypeAll: Concealment of adverse events from FDA
cases.SchemeSummary: Ilic, ExThera's Chief Regulatory Officer, intentionally failed to file required adverse event reports with the FDA - including the deaths of two patients treated with ExThera's blood filtration device at an Antigua clinic used by U.S. cancer patients - to avoid regulatory scrutiny and preserve clinical trial partnerships and financial prospects; ExThera admitted acting through Ilic and entered a three-year deferred prosecution agreement with a $750,000 criminal penalty plus a $5,694,750 forfeiture order, while Ilic agreed to plead guilty and awaits sentencing.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
cases.FraudEntity: China Jushi USA Corp. (South Carolina corporation; subsidiary of China Jushi Corp.)
cases.PayerName: U.S. Small Business Administration (Paycheck Protection Program)
cases.SchemeSummary: China Jushi USA falsely certified in its first-draw PPP loan application that it was eligible for the program when, counting affiliates' employees, it exceeded the applicable SBA size standards; it obtained and had forgiven a PPP loan totaling $3,590,007 (with interest) and caused the government to pay $35,581 in lender processing fees. The company paid $5,075,823 to resolve False Claims Act allegations in a qui tam suit, with the relator receiving $507,582.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Florida
cases.FraudEntity: Absolute Physical & Aquatic Therapy, LLC; Chipley Physical Therapy, LLC; Ruben Laurel (owner/operator); Lorrie Laurel (owner/operator, physical therapist)
cases.State_County: Florida - Washington County (Chipley); Florida - Jackson County (Marianna); Florida - Holmes County (Bonifay)
cases.SchemeSummary: Defendants submitted 503 claims to federal health care programs for outpatient physical therapy services purportedly rendered by physical therapist Lorrie Laurel on dates when she was actually out of the country on cruises to Mexico, Jamaica, Aruba and the Bahamas; the FCA settlement of $754,722.88 (including $19,988.34 restitution) resolved a qui tam action by a former employee who receives $150,944.58.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
cases.FraudEntity: Teflyon Cameron (chiropractor; owner/operator with financial interest in DME and CGx companies)
cases.State_County: Georgia - Powder Springs (Cobb County); New Jersey
cases.SchemeSummary: Cameron and conspirators owned DME and cancer genetic testing (CGx) companies, used marketing call centers and telemedicine companies to obtain doctors' orders for orthotic braces regardless of medical necessity, and billed Medicare; she also sold beneficiary leads to a clinical laboratory on a per-lead basis disguised by a sham agreement, causing over $14.9 million in Medicare losses and personally netting more than $1.3 million.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Delaware
cases.FraudEntity: Alpha Care Medical, LLC; Nihar Gala (owner); Bo Wang (laboratory director)
cases.State_County: Delaware - Sussex County (Lewes); Pennsylvania - Delaware County (Glen Mills)
cases.PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; TRICARE; Federal Employees Health Benefits Program
cases.SchemeSummary: The United States filed a False Claims Act civil complaint alleging that a medical practice, its owner, and its laboratory director submitted thousands of claims to Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE and FEHBP for laboratory diagnostic tests that had no valid medical purpose for diagnosis or treatment, were performed in violation of clinical laboratory reliability standards, and in numerous instances were never performed at all.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Kentucky
cases.FraudEntity: Access Adult Health Day Care Center LLC (Access); Encore AHDC LLC (Encore); Tatyanas Case Management LLC (TCM); Serge Adamov (owner of Access); Inna Frimerman (owner of Encore); Tatyana Kolesnikova (owner of TCM)
cases.PayerName: Kentucky Medicaid (Home and Community Based Waiver Program)
cases.SchemeSummary: Three commonly-owned Kentucky Medicaid HCB Waiver providers and their owners allegedly used shared financial interests to steer waiver beneficiaries from the case-management company (required to be conflict-free) to their own attendant-care agencies, which then billed Kentucky Medicaid for in-home attendant care hours that were partly or entirely not provided; the six defendants collectively agreed to pay $23,816,217.60 under the False Claims Act to resolve a qui tam suit, with a Corporate Integrity Agreement for Kolesnikova and TCM.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
cases.FraudEntity: Jerry Dale Leech (chiropractor, owner of Midwest Marketing); Dr. Stanley L. Librach (physician); Dr. Asim Muhammad Ali (physician, operator of Central Diagnostic Laboratory); Denis J. Mikhlin (co-defendant, business owner); Central Diagnostic Laboratory
cases.State_County: Missouri - St. Louis County (Clayton, Chesterfield, Creve Coeur); Missouri - St. Louis
cases.SchemeSummary: Chiropractor Leech directed a scheme in which physicians Ali and Librach wrote oxycodone and other controlled-substance prescriptions (at least 94,971 pills) without examining patients or reviewing charts and with no legitimate medical purpose, knowing pharmacies would bill Medicare and Medicaid; Leech also traded fraudulent prescriptions for cash. Separately, urine samples were steered to Dr. Ali's Central Diagnostic Laboratory, which billed Medicare and Medicaid at least $861,600 for testing and paid at least $150,795 in kickbacks to Leech's Midwest Marketing and entities of co-defendant Mikhlin. Restitution figures span four defendants (Leech $4.7M, Librach $2.87M, Ali $1.8M, Mikhlin $181,265); longest sentence was Mikhlin's nine years.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Ohio
cases.FraudEntity: Sherita Booker (tax return preparer, owner of tax preparation business)
cases.SchemeSummary: Booker, who ran her own tax preparation business, allegedly prepared and filed false federal income tax returns for clients by attaching fabricated Schedule C business profit/loss forms to their Form 1040s even though the clients owned no businesses, along with other schemes to reduce tax owed to the IRS. No health care payer is involved.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York
cases.FraudEntity: Olga Popovych (office manager of several physical therapy clinics)
cases.SchemeSummary: Popovych managed Brooklyn physical therapy clinics that paid cash kickbacks to ambulette drivers to recruit and transport Medicare patients to the clinics, and she falsified medical records to show that physical therapists who were not present had treated the patients; Medicare paid the clinics over $8 million between 2018 and 2020.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York; U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York; DOJ Criminal Division Fraud Section / National Fraud Enforcement Division
cases.FraudEntity: Olga Popovych (office manager of several physical therapy clinics)
cases.State_County: New York - New York County (New York City)
cases.SchemeSummary: Popovych, office manager of physical therapy clinics, paid cash kickbacks to ambulette drivers who recruited Medicare beneficiaries to the clinics, and falsified medical records to show that physical therapists who were not present had treated the patients; Medicare paid the clinics over $8 million between 2018 and 2020.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York; Justice Department National Fraud Enforcement Division / U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York
cases.FraudEntity: Tony Brown-Arkah (owner, American Medical Centers); American Medical Centers (AMC)
cases.SchemeSummary: Brown-Arkah owned a Brooklyn clinic purporting to provide substance abuse treatment; he lured patients with Suboxone prescriptions signed by a Florida-based nurse practitioner who never saw the patients, required medically unnecessary invasive testing, and billed Medicare and Medicaid over $52 million for services never provided, including office visits where he, a non-provider, was the only staff to see the patient. He paid cash kickbacks to patients for referrals and received monthly kickbacks from a laboratory for referring medically unnecessary tests, concealing them via a shell company and sham contract, while allowing diversion/sale of Suboxone prescriptions at the clinic.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Washington
cases.FraudEntity: Dr. David Antonio Becerril (physician); Real Time Physicians, LLC (telemedicine/telemarketing company)
cases.State_County: Idaho - Kootenai County (Coeur d'Alene); Washington (Eastern District)
cases.SchemeSummary: While contracting with telemarketing/telemedicine company Real Time Physicians, Becerril signed false orders and medical-necessity attestations for genetic tests and DME braces (back, knee, shoulder, ankle) for elderly Medicare beneficiaries he never contacted - including deceased patients and amputees - reviewing each prescription for about 26 seconds and receiving $20 per signed prescription, which were used to bill Medicare roughly $1.25 million.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Colorado
cases.FraudEntity: Mohamed Elias Omer (operator of Nadina Adult Daycare Center, LLC); Nadina Adult Daycare Center, LLC
cases.PayerName: Medicaid (Colorado Department of Health Care Policy and Financing)
cases.SchemeSummary: Omer was indicted on twelve counts of illegal remuneration for allegedly paying kickbacks - three $500 payments plus about $10,000 disguised as 'marketing expenses' or 'office supply' - to induce referrals of Medicaid beneficiaries to attend his Arapahoe County adult daycare center, whose services were billed to Colorado Medicaid.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
cases.FraudEntity: Dr. Jonathan Wayne Morris (medical doctor, owner of Columbia Urgent Care)
cases.SchemeSummary: Indictment alleges the clinic owner billed Medicare and Missouri Medicaid for services as if he personally provided them when they were actually rendered by unsupervised, untrained assistant physicians, and also submitted claims for controlled substance prescriptions issued outside the usual course of professional practice to friends, people with substance use disorders, and sexual partners, sometimes for cash.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
cases.FraudEntity: Coastal Diagnostics, LLC (reference laboratory); Tricia Conroy (owner)
cases.SchemeSummary: Conroy falsely answered 'No' on Coastal Diagnostics' Connecticut Medicaid Provider Enrollment Application when asked whether any owner was related by family or business relationship to another enrolled provider, concealing ties to Genco Lab (owned by her husband, at the same address, then under payment suspension and fraud investigation); Medicaid would not have enrolled Coastal had the truth been disclosed, making the lab's subsequent claims for laboratory services false. Coastal and Conroy paid $145,720 covering March 6 to June 3, 2024.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania; U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania
cases.FraudEntity: Segal Arts, LLC; Irina Segal (sole owner and manager)
cases.SchemeSummary: Segal Arts and its owner allegedly billed Medicare under a CPT code for one-on-one skilled therapeutic exercise/occupational therapy while actually providing only group arts-and-crafts sessions to beneficiaries at assisted living and adult day facilities in Pennsylvania and New Jersey, and failed to repay Medicare for the non-covered group sessions even after HHS-OIG agents educated the owner on the code's individual skilled-therapy requirements; a consent judgment requires repayment of $200,000 based on ability to pay.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
cases.FraudEntity: Phillips-Glenwood Construction, Inc. (Vernon, New Jersey contractor)
cases.SchemeSummary: Under contracts for construction and facilities maintenance of USPS facilities in New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Delaware, the company allegedly submitted false and altered documentation that inflated its labor hours and materials purchases in requests for payment, obtaining overpayments from the Postal Service; resolved by a $2.4 million False Claims Act settlement.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
cases.FraudEntity: Coretta "Cory" Elliott (owner/operator of CMT LLC, d/b/a CMT Roofing LLC); CMT LLC
cases.SchemeSummary: Elliott obtained a $875,000 first-draw and $833,333 second-draw Paycheck Protection Program loan for her construction company by inflating reported monthly payroll and falsely certifying the funds would be used for business purposes, then obtained loan forgiveness with false claims about payroll spending; she diverted $200,000 to a personal investment account, $559,455 to company union dues, and other funds to personal uses.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
cases.FraudEntity: Sabrina Mitlo (purported business owner); Joseph Mitlo (purported business owner)
cases.SchemeSummary: The married couple allegedly submitted fraudulent Paycheck Protection Program loan applications for two New Jersey businesses they purportedly owned that had no employees or payroll, supporting the applications with falsified tax documents showing prior wage payments; after over $715,000 in loans were deposited, they used a payroll service to issue checks to purported employees who did not work for the businesses, and Sabrina Mitlo cashed those checks at a check cashing facility and kept the proceeds.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Kentucky
cases.FraudEntity: Matthew Ryan Elkins (contract certified registered nurse anesthetist at a Louisville pain treatment center)
cases.State_County: Kentucky - Jefferson County (Louisville); Kentucky - Oldham County (Crestwood)
cases.SchemeSummary: A contract nurse anesthetist burglarized the pain clinic where he worked, twice weekly for at least three months, emptying patient-specific pre-filled syringes of intrathecal pain medication into a separate vial for his own use and refilling the syringes with sodium chloride before returning them to the office safe, so patients with implanted pain pumps received diluted, adulterated medication and suffered pain and withdrawal. He was sentenced to 77 months, fined $15,000, and forfeited his Kentucky nursing licenses.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
cases.SchemeSummary: Not a single-defendant case: this is the Fraud Section's 2025 Year in Review announcement, reporting the largest health care fraud takedown in DOJ history with defendants charged with more than $14.6 billion in intended loss, over 260 defendants charged for economic crimes overall, 25 trials, and 15 corporate enforcement actions (four health care related) totaling over $1 billion in global monetary resolutions.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
cases.FraudEntity: Tania Rosa Rodriguez (participant in healthcare fraud conspiracy; naturalization applicant)
cases.SchemeSummary: Rodriguez participated in a seven-year healthcare fraud conspiracy that generated roughly $4.6 million in fraudulent healthcare claims (for which she was separately convicted), and concealed that criminal conduct on her 2017 naturalization application by stating she had never committed a crime for which she had not been arrested, obtaining U.S. citizenship in 2018; the jury convicted her of unlawful procurement of citizenship or naturalization.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia
cases.FraudEntity: Steven A. Price (dentist, operator of Washington Smile Center); Keidi C. Moore (dental hygienist)
cases.SchemeSummary: A dentist and his hygienist submitted repeated D.C. Medicaid reimbursement claims for clinical crown lengthening procedures and space maintainers that were never performed, in some cases billing more than 30 crown lengthenings and more than 20 space maintainers for a single patient over a few years, causing over $4 million in payouts.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice - Civil Division; U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Texas
cases.FraudEntity: Magnolia Diagnostics (clinical laboratory); John Bains (owner); Kelly Bains (owner); Magnolia Diagnostics investors
cases.SchemeSummary: Lab required senior living communities seeking COVID-19 testing to also receive expensive respiratory pathogen panels, using prepopulated requisition forms with preselected RPP tests and diagnosis codes treated as blanket standing orders (two allegedly altered to cover additional facilities), and ran RPPs on frozen specimens weeks or months later, billing Medicare for thousands of medically unnecessary panels; owners and lab pay $19.2M and investors an additional $4.8M.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Wisconsin
cases.FraudEntity: Bruce Johnson (co-owner, Kestrel Medical LLC); Michael Comino (50% owner, Kestrel Medical LLC); Kestrel Medical LLC (DME supplier)
cases.SchemeSummary: Owners of a durable medical equipment company paid kickbacks to purported marketing companies in exchange for signed doctors' orders/prescriptions for orthotic braces, which Kestrel then billed to Medicare, collecting over $2 million; Johnson also transferred $150,000 to a company of his co-defendant to divest Kestrel of assets before bankruptcy. Johnson received 18 months and over $2 million restitution; co-defendant Comino received 22 months plus restitution.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division (Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section) and U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia
cases.FraudEntity: DISH Wireless LLC (wholly owned subsidiary of EchoStar Corporation, operating Boost Mobile)
cases.State_County: Colorado - Englewood (company headquarters); internal sales employees in Texas, Florida, New York and West Virginia
cases.PayerName: Federal Communications Commission - Emergency Broadband Benefit Program (EBBP) and Affordable Connectivity Program (ACP)
cases.SchemeSummary: DISH enrolled more than 130,000 subscribers into the FCC's EBBP and ACP broadband subsidy programs based on purported attendance at Community Eligibility Provision schools, collecting up to $50 per subscriber per month (EBBP) and $30 per month (ACP); internal sales staff trained third-party agents to submit applications with incorrect school information, resulting in over 16,000 households enrolled on the basis of schools more than 25 miles away with no verified attendance, 130 households using dependents over age 21, more than 66,000 subscribers with no school-aged student identified, and over 2,400 duplicate beneficiaries, with executives failing to correct the problem from September 2021 through April 2022.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Arizona
cases.FraudEntity: Susie Kamien (medical biller); Jimmy Muyumbu (owner/operator, Motherland Counseling LLC); Sandra Peters (sales representative); Brian Rowan (Vice President of Sales, amniotic wound allograft company)
cases.PayerName: Medicare; Arizona Medicaid (Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System - AHCCCS); TRICARE; CHAMPVA; commercial insurers
cases.SchemeSummary: Four defendants charged in the District of Arizona in schemes totaling over $1.2 billion: Rowan, a VP of Sales for an amniotic wound allograft company, allegedly paid hundreds of millions in kickbacks, bribes and rebates to sales reps and providers, concealed via sham inflated invoices and shell-company pass-through accounts, causing medically unnecessary allografts to be applied to elderly and hospice patients and $1.2 billion in claims to Medicare, TRICARE, CHAMPVA and commercial insurers (about $614 million paid, Rowan personally netting over $24 million); biller Kamien submitted over $918 million and sales rep Peters over $10 million in allograft claims that were medically unnecessary and kickback-tainted; Muyumbu billed AHCCCS approximately $44.9 million (about $36.7 million paid) through a Phoenix substance-abuse clinic for services not provided or so substandard as to have no treatment value, targeting Native American members of the American Indian Health Program, and laundered proceeds into Phoenix-area real estate.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division and U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: Dr. Pankaj Merchia (sleep medicine physician, controlled several sleep medicine companies)
cases.State_County: Massachusetts - Norfolk County (Brookline); Massachusetts - Suffolk County (Boston); Florida - Palm Beach County (Boca Raton)
cases.PayerName: Private health insurance companies (unnamed commercial insurers)
cases.SchemeSummary: From 2017 to 2019 Merchia billed commercial insurers millions of dollars — up to hundreds of thousands per patient — for sleep apnea machines that his former patients had not used for years and in some cases had returned to him, using proceeds to buy a $2.1 million Brookline home; he separately billed over $390,000 (the only quantified insurance figure) for treating his own brother, and after being told he could not bill for a family member, created a new medical business in a nominee's name to keep the payments flowing. He also failed to report over $6.5 million in income from 2009 to 2019 by falsely claiming a co-conspirator owned the businesses via a sham 2008 sale.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Washington
cases.FraudEntity: FidaLab, LLC (Seattle medical testing laboratory)
cases.SchemeSummary: FidaLab sought permission to bill a series of urinary tract infection tests as a single panel; after that request was denied, it billed the same tests under multiple separate billing codes instead of one code, inflating charges to Medicare. The lab paid $2 million to resolve the False Claims Act allegations without admitting fault and agreed not to bill patients for the unallowed costs.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Rhode Island
cases.FraudEntity: William Jose Alejandro Arias Amador
cases.SchemeSummary: Defendant, a Dominican national residing in Providence, used a U.S. citizen's identity and Social Security number to apply for and obtain Medicaid and SNAP benefits for which he was ineligible; he pleaded guilty to false representation of a Social Security number, health care fraud and wire fraud.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Rhode Island
cases.FraudEntity: Jesus Matos Perez (beneficiary; Dominican national residing illegally in the U.S.)
cases.SchemeSummary: For roughly ten years the defendant used the stolen identities, dates of birth and Social Security numbers of two U.S. citizens to enroll in and collect approximately $75,000 in combined Medicaid, SNAP and unemployment benefits for which he was not eligible; he pleaded guilty to illegal entry, false representation of a Social Security number, health care fraud and wire fraud.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
cases.FraudEntity: Juan Francisco De La Cruz Mejia (Dominican national, beneficiary)
cases.PayerName: Medicare; Social Security Administration (Title II disability benefits)
cases.SchemeSummary: Defendant used a stolen U.S. citizen's name and Social Security number to collect $105,057.90 in Social Security Title II disability benefits and to enroll in Medicare in April 2021; under that stolen identity he obtained medical services, prescription drugs and DME, causing providers to bill Medicare Parts A, B and D approximately $3.4 million, of which Medicare paid about $108,057.63.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Rhode Island
cases.FraudEntity: Jesus Matos Perez (Dominican national, benefits recipient using stolen identities); William Jose Alejandro Arias Amador (Dominican national, benefits recipient using stolen identity)
cases.SchemeSummary: Two Dominican nationals used stolen Social Security numbers and identities of U.S. citizens to enroll in and receive Medicaid, SNAP and unemployment benefits they were ineligible for; Matos Perez obtained roughly $75,000 in benefits over about ten years using two stolen identities and received 18 months, while Arias Amador used a stolen identity to obtain Medicaid and SNAP benefits and received 12 months and one day.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
cases.FraudEntity: Joseph Pizzo (Medicaid recipient); Tiziana Taormina (personal care aide); Donna Romsteadt (Medicaid recipient); Alyssa Cuculino (home care aide); Louise Israel (home care aide); Elexis Cuculino (Medicaid recipient); Albert Coccia Jr. (Medicaid recipient); Santino Coccia (home care aide); Sean Murray (home care worker); Charles Bowie (home care worker); Khaleelah Williams (owner, Benevolent Home Health LLC); Saleemah Davis (owner, Benevolent Home Health LLC); Benevolent Home Health LLC (home care agency)
cases.State_County: Pennsylvania - Philadelphia County (Philadelphia); Pennsylvania - Bucks County
cases.SchemeSummary: Across three federal cases (plus related state charges), home care aides and Medicaid recipients allegedly submitted false clock-ins and billed Pennsylvania Medicaid for personal home care services never rendered - claiming hours while aides were incarcerated, hospitalized, working other jobs (construction, rideshare/food delivery), vacationing overseas (Saudi Arabia, Jamaica, Colombia), trafficking drugs, or even deceased. Amounts span multiple defendants: approx. $160,000 (Pizzo/Taormina), $445,000 (Romsteadt et al.), $211,000 (Coccias), $400,000 (Murray, who also paid kickbacks to clients to participate), $600,000 (Bowie), and $224,000 (Williams/Davis/Benevolent Home Health), with the overall announced total of $5.76 million in Medicaid billings including state cases.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
cases.FraudEntity: Shiva Akula (owner of healthcare agencies)
cases.SchemeSummary: Annual collections announcement; the only health care matter described is defendant Shiva Akula, who was found guilty at trial of health care fraud (18 U.S.C. § 1347), with approximately $4.7 million in restitution to Medicare collected between October 2024 and April 2025 through Writs of Execution and the sale of his healthcare agencies. The document does not describe the billing mechanics of the underlying scheme.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Iowa
cases.FraudEntity: Eric Leo Newsom (licensed occupational therapist; owner/operator of occupational therapy company)
cases.SchemeSummary: A licensed occupational therapist diverted narcotics from current and former patients: he picked up an elderly hospice patient's hydrocodone prescription from a pharmacy and substituted score-marked zinc tablets in the container, leaving her without pain medication for two days before her death; he also burglarized assisted-living apartments to steal narcotics from other residents.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Oklahoma
cases.FraudEntity: Edward Shadid, MD (board-certified spinal surgeon; operator of Spine & Pain Care of Oklahoma clinics in Edmond and Lawton)
cases.SchemeSummary: The United States alleged that Dr. Shadid transferred Schedule II controlled substances between his Edmond and Lawton clinics without using DEA Form 222s, failed to keep accurate records of Schedule IV transfers, did not obtain a separate DEA registration for the Lawton clinic, and failed to maintain a biennial inventory; he paid $110,000 in civil penalties without admitting liability.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Texas
cases.FraudEntity: Dr. Brian August (physician)
cases.SchemeSummary: Dr. August allegedly issued 255 controlled substance prescriptions (Schedule II and IV opioids, benzodiazepines and other drugs) to 15 patients without a legitimate medical purpose, documented medical necessity, or compliance with Texas pain-treatment requirements; because the patients were Medicare Part D and/or Texas Medicaid beneficiaries, the resulting pharmacy claims were not reimbursable. He paid $200,000, including $44,380.55 restitution to Medicare Part D and $994.22 to Texas Medicaid, and surrendered his DEA registration and medical license.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: The Mitchell Eye Center (Florida ophthalmology practice); Dr. Alan Mitchell (ophthalmologist and former owner)
cases.SchemeSummary: Mitchell Eye Center received per-referral payments from diagnostics company Eyecuity, PLLC (disguised as fair-market-value rent and administrative service payments) for referring patients for transcranial doppler (TCD) tests, and its physicians signed Eyecuity-supplied order forms falsely documenting a rare Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency diagnosis to establish medical necessity so Eyecuity could bill Medicare and the VA for the unnecessary tests.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division (Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section) and U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts; U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: EyePoint Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (pharmaceutical manufacturer, headquartered in Massachusetts)
cases.SchemeSummary: After launching DEXYCU, an injectable drug for ocular inflammation after cataract surgery, EyePoint allegedly induced Ambulatory Surgery Centers to purchase and dispense the drug by running an 'Assurance Program' that reimbursed or compensated ASCs when insurers denied claims or paid below the ASCs' acquisition cost, and by giving excessive free samples, resulting in tainted claims to federal health care programs; resolved by a $4,657,463.18 federal payment plus $21,518.68 to participating states and a five-year Corporate Integrity Agreement, with the qui tam relator AFCE LLC receiving $791,768.74.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division, Office of Public Affairs
cases.SchemeSummary: Annual Justice Department statistical report, not an individual case: False Claims Act settlements and judgments exceeded $6.8 billion in fiscal year 2025, of which over $5.7 billion involved the health care industry (federal losses to Medicare, Medicaid and TRICARE), with emphasis on managed care, prescription drug, and medically unnecessary care matters; 1,297 qui tam suits were filed and qui tam-related recoveries exceeded $5.3 billion.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of North Carolina
cases.FraudEntity: Ronald Ray Brock II (applicant/owner); MedCom Medical Messaging, Inc.; Physicians Answering Group Exchange, Inc.; Answer Pronto, Inc.
cases.PayerName: U.S. Small Business Administration (Paycheck Protection Program)
cases.SchemeSummary: Brock allegedly obtained $996,668.50 in PPP loans in the names of three shell companies (medical answering/messaging businesses) by falsely claiming they had 14-57 employees and monthly payroll of $32,000-$121,000, when the companies had no operations, employees or payroll; he supported the applications with fabricated tax returns and other falsified documents, obtained duplicate loans for one company through two lenders, and made further false statements to obtain SBA loan forgiveness.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Wisconsin
cases.FraudEntity: Jasmine Cooper (operator of a prenatal care coordination agency); Jerry Jones III (physician/DEA-registered prescriber)
cases.State_County: Wisconsin - Milwaukee County (Brown Deer); Wisconsin - Ozaukee County (Mequon)
cases.SchemeSummary: Cooper, authorized to operate a prenatal care coordination agency serving at-risk pregnant women, submitted thousands of false claims to Wisconsin Medicaid for services beneficiaries never received and misstated the duration, frequency, date and nature of services, billing over $5.8 million and being paid over $5.4 million, and used another person's means of identification without authority. Separately charged in the same announcement, Dr. Jerry Jones III conspired to distribute Adderall, Ritalin and other controlled substances outside the usual course of professional practice, agreeing to forfeit $294,850.72 in proceeds; the office noted four similar prenatal care coordination schemes costing Wisconsin Medicaid over $15.5 million in total.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Colorado (with the Colorado Attorney General's Office / Medicaid Fraud, Abuse & Neglect Unit)
cases.FraudEntity: Ashley Marie Stevens (owner, Armistead Twin Rides, LLC); Wesam Yassin (owner, Sama Limo)
cases.State_County: Colorado - Mesa County; Colorado - Douglas County
cases.SchemeSummary: Two separately indicted non-emergent medical transportation (NEMT) providers billed Colorado Medicaid for rides that never occurred or had no related medical appointment: Stevens billed over $1 million through Armistead Twin Rides, including more than $400,000 for rides for herself and family, over $150,000 for rides that did not occur or went to non-medical destinations, and more than $450,000 for purported 400+ mile trips; Yassin billed about $3.3 million through Sama Limo, including roughly $283,000 for 64 rides for one beneficiary of which about $165,000 was for rides billed after the beneficiary's death. Proceeds were allegedly spent on a luxury vehicle, a home, jewelry, travel and cosmetic surgery (figures span both defendants).

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Tennessee
cases.FraudEntity: Yoshi Dawn Matthews (tax preparer); Ricky Darnell Matthews (operator of DYM Financial Services); DYM Financial Services; Julie Robinson Wade (business owner, granite fabrication company)
cases.SchemeSummary: Two separate indictments announced together: Yoshi Dawn Matthews prepared and filed federal income tax returns for clients between February 2019 and January 2023 falsely claiming the fuel tax credit (asserting taxpayers used hundreds of thousands of gallons of fuel), filed through DYM Financial Services operated by her son Ricky Darnell Matthews, causing an approximate $1,438,000 tax loss; separately, Julie Robinson Wade allegedly failed to file quarterly employment tax returns and failed to pay over approximately $147,676 in income, Medicare and Social Security taxes withheld from her granite company's employees (2019-2022). No health care payer was involved.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Missouri
cases.FraudEntity: Darcee Jo Heath (purported graduate practical nurse); Romond E. Holt (personal care services provider); Carolyn S. McGinnis (Medicaid recipient); Kevin E. Oliver (personal care services provider)
cases.State_County: Missouri - Camden County (Linn Creek); Missouri - Jackson County (Kansas City, Independence); Missouri - Ray County (Richmond)
cases.SchemeSummary: Three defendants allegedly submitted false Missouri Medicaid claims for personal care services never rendered because the recipients were hospitalized or in long-term rehabilitation facilities: Holt filed 32 claims ($4,743.61), McGinnis filed 35 claims for an attendant who was not providing care while she was not living at home ($3,022.94), and Oliver filed 82 claims ($6,171.40). A fourth defendant, Heath, allegedly forged college records and a nursing diploma to obtain hospital employment as a graduate practical nurse. Figures span multiple defendants; announced as part of the 2026 National Health Care Fraud Takedown charging 455 defendants nationwide with over $6.5 billion in false claims.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Tennessee
cases.FraudEntity: Tiffany Haney; Anne Warren; Tina Roper; Rocky Hill Pharmacy
cases.SchemeSummary: Three women associated with Rocky Hill Pharmacy altered healthcare providers' prescriptions without authorization to add medications, and submitted claims to Medicare, TennCare and other payors for the added drugs; some prescriptions were fabricated entirely using providers' names/identities without authorization.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Tennessee
cases.FraudEntity: Sanjeev Kumar (physician/gynecologic oncologist, operator of Poplar Avenue Clinic)
cases.SchemeSummary: Kumar and the advanced practitioners he supervised performed over 15,000 in-office hysteroscopy-with-biopsy procedures on 5,559 Medicare and Medicaid patients between September 2019 and April 2024, billing more than $41 million (netting over $4.8 million from Medicare and Medicaid) for procedures that were not medically necessary and were performed with adulterated, improperly reprocessed or reused single-use hysteroscopes and graspers.
