A related release notes he was later sentenced to 20 years in prison.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of California
cases.FraudEntity: Cindy Justice (owner and president of PureScience Rx); Ashleigh Davis (operations manager, licensed pharmacy technician); PureScience Rx (pharmacy)
cases.SchemeSummary: Owners of a Poway pharmacy paid marketers commissions based on Medicare reimbursements for prescriptions generated by telemarketing call centers and sham telehealth encounters with no legitimate examination, concealing the kickbacks with sham contracts and fabricated hourly invoices; many prescriptions were issued using stolen nurse practitioner identities, and expensive medically unnecessary drugs (including non-FDA-approved 'footbath' drugs) were billed to Medicare, which paid over $4.9 million.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of North Carolina
cases.FraudEntity: Murad "Mike" Ayyad (owner/controller of laboratories and other entities)
cases.PayerName: Medicare; Health Resources Services Administration (HRSA); TRICARE; other payers
cases.SchemeSummary: Ayyad allegedly solicited and received kickbacks from clinical laboratories (including two in which he had de facto ownership) in exchange for generating referrals for laboratory testing billed to Medicare, HRSA and TRICARE, and paid kickbacks (meals, cash and in-kind payments) to independent contractor sales reps and providers to induce referrals; dozens of sham invoices and contracts were created to conceal the payments, at least one of which was given to federal investigators.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of New York
cases.FraudEntity: Joseph Carl (owner/manager, Carl's Cab); Randolph Ekstrom (manager, Carl's Cab); Muhammad Zishan (manager, Latham Taxi Inc.); Madiha Javed (manager, Latham Taxi Inc.); Ghazali Shaikh (manager, Latham Taxi Inc.); Douglas C. Cline, M.D. P.C. d/b/a Chronic Pain Management; Douglas C. Cline, M.D. (owner); Laurie McKenna (nurse practitioner); Aptihealth Inc. and Aptihealth Medical, PLLC (telehealth behavioral health provider)
cases.State_County: New York - Saratoga County (Clifton Park, Saratoga Springs); New York - Montgomery County (Canajoharie); New York - Warren County (Glens Falls, Queensbury, Bolton Landing); New York - Albany County (Latham)
cases.SchemeSummary: Two Medicaid non-emergency transportation companies (Carl's Cab and Latham Taxi Inc.) allegedly paid Medicaid recipients cash, controlled substances and other things of value to induce them to use their rides to medical appointments including methadone clinics, and the Latham Taxi defendants also allegedly falsified trip data to overbill and bill for trips never provided, obtaining $4,296,374.02 and $666,281.42 in Medicaid reimbursements respectively; separately, a pain clinic and its owner/nurse practitioner paid $500,000 to resolve allegations of prescribing high-dose opioids tied to recurring cash payments without adequate oversight, and a telehealth behavioral health provider paid $300,000 over billing Medicare/Medicaid for services not rendered or undocumented, billing administrative tasks as medical services, and giving gift cards to induce recipients to receive services.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division and U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
cases.FraudEntity: Clay Eye Holdings LLC (ophthalmology practice); Retina Macula Specialist of Miami LLC (ophthalmology practice); Florida Eye Institute P.A. (ophthalmology practice); Miami Eye LLC (ophthalmology practice); Kendall Eye Institute Inc. (ophthalmology practice)
cases.SchemeSummary: Five Florida ophthalmology practices performed trans-cranial doppler ultrasounds (TCDs) on thousands of patients and billed Medicare and Medicaid hundreds of dollars per test, attributing to patients a serious qualifying diagnosis that nearly none of them actually had and that appeared neither in their medical history nor in the TCD results; the practices paid a third-party testing company based on the volume or value of tests ordered and referred patients to that company's preferred radiology group for the professional component, in alleged violation of the Anti-Kickback Statute and Stark Law. Settlement figures total $5,975,000 across the five practices, of which $333,500 goes to Florida's Medicaid share and $1,135,250 to the qui tam whistleblower.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: Simon Grinshteyn (Florida-based doctor)
cases.SchemeSummary: Grinshteyn worked with a purported telemedicine company and signed pre-populated medical records and doctors' orders for medically unnecessary genetic testing and DME for Medicare beneficiaries he never contacted or examined; DME suppliers and laboratories then used the signed orders to bill Medicare, which paid over $3.1 million.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division, Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section
cases.FraudEntity: NeoGenomics Laboratories Inc. (clinical laboratory)
cases.SchemeSummary: The government alleged NeoGenomics, through its Laboratory Clinical Initiative, gave 28 health care providers laboratory consulting services (to set up in-house flow cytometry and FISH capabilities) at below fair market value to induce referrals of clinical laboratory tests, and paid independent consultants compensation varying with the volume or value of referrals for identifying provider customers, violating the Anti-Kickback Statute and Stark Law; NeoGenomics self-disclosed and paid $9,813,260.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
cases.FraudEntity: Sean Alterman (owner/operator of Live Beyond Medical MGMT, LLC and Dynix Diagnostics LLC); Live Beyond Medical MGMT, LLC; Dynix Diagnostics LLC; Shivv LLC (shell company); Shank LLC (shell company)
cases.SchemeSummary: Alterman's two labs bought doctors' orders for expensive genetic tests from patient recruiters who used deceptive telemarketing and 'doctor chasing' faxes falsely claiming a mutual patient relationship to get physicians to sign prescriptions for medically unnecessary tests; the labs billed Medicare about $52 million and were paid about $36 million, with roughly $5.5 million flowing to Alterman through shell companies Shivv LLC and Shank LLC. He agreed to forfeit his Lake Worth estate and a 2022 Rolls Royce Ghost.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; USAO - Southern District of Florida
cases.FraudEntity: Sean Alterman (owner/operator of laboratories); Live Beyond Medical MGMT, LLC; Dynix Diagnostics LLC; Shivv LLC; Shank LLC
cases.SchemeSummary: Alterman's two labs purchased doctors' orders for expensive genetic tests from patient recruiters who used deceptive telemarketing and 'doctor chasing' faxes falsely claiming a mutual patient to trick physicians into signing prescriptions for medically unnecessary tests; the labs billed Medicare about $52 million and were paid about $36 million, with roughly $5.5 million routed to Alterman through shell companies, and he agreed to forfeit his estate and a 2022 Rolls Royce Ghost.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Pennsylvania
cases.FraudEntity: Frank Suess (a.k.a. Franz P. Suess) (financier/controller of pharmacies, Medivalue Florida LLC); Luis Salgado (MedX Marketing Solutions); Melissa Driscoll (Sterling Pharmacy purchaser); Victor Velazco; Dave Singh; Warren Pizik; Diana Castro
cases.State_County: Pennsylvania - Lackawanna County (Jermyn); Pennsylvania - Monroe County (East Stroudsburg); Florida - Palm Beach County (Wellington); New York
cases.PayerName: Medicare; Medicare-sponsored prescription drug plans; private health insurance fund
cases.SchemeSummary: Suess secretly financed and controlled pharmacies (Sterling in PA, DCE in TX, Motto in FL) and steered high-cost mail-order prescription 'foot bath' drug combinations (vancomycin, tobramycin, moxifloxacin drops, etc.) to them, billing private insurance, Medicare and Medicare Part D for medically unnecessary drugs ordered via prechecked, templated forms collected at New York 'health fairs' with no patient evaluation; kickbacks were paid for signed order forms and disguised as an hourly 'marketing services agreement' with codefendant Salgado's MedX Marketing Solutions, and a false compliance document was created to obstruct the investigation. The $700,000 profit figure relates to the conspiracy's fraudulent foot bath orders from one private insurance fund; Suess forfeits a Florida property valued at about $4 million.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: Deane Gilmore (owner and manager of Jupiter Medical Associates Inc. and Granite Medical Associates Inc.); Jupiter Medical Associates Inc.; Granite Medical Associates Inc.
cases.SchemeSummary: Gilmore, through two durable medical equipment companies he owned, paid telemarketers/call centers on a per-order basis for DME orders (back, knee, wrist, ankle braces) generated from Medicare beneficiaries' medical information, with documentation making it appear practitioners had legitimately prescribed the braces though the orders were often medically unnecessary and based on false documentation; approximately $6.5 million in kickback-tainted claims were submitted to Medicare, which paid about $2.3 million.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Indiana
cases.FraudEntity: Justyn Arch (vice president of a dental practice)
cases.State_County: Indiana - Porter County (Chesterton); Indiana - Lake County (Crown Point)
cases.SchemeSummary: As vice president of a dental practice with locations in Chesterton and Crown Point, Indiana, Arch submitted claims to Indiana Medicaid for hundreds of dental surgeries that were never performed, using patients' personal identifiers without authorization to support the fraudulent claims, and evaded taxes on the resulting income; restitution of $520,897 covers the Medicaid and IRS losses combined.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
cases.FraudEntity: Ted Albin (operator of Grapevine Professional Services, medical billing company); Grapevine Professional Services; Erin Foley (co-owner of DME supply companies)
cases.SchemeSummary: Albin ran a medical billing company that submitted thousands of Medicare reimbursement claims for durable medical equipment (back, knee, wrist and shoulder braces) on behalf of DME supply companies, including ones he and his sister owned, based on prescriptions illegally purchased with kickbacks and often bearing forged doctor signatures and no medical necessity; the DME companies billed Medicare over $38 million and were paid over $12 million.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
cases.FraudEntity: Christian "Chris" Cruz (nursing assistant; owner/operator of a Florida durable medical equipment supplier); unnamed co-conspirator (co-owner, convicted felon, charged and at large)
cases.SchemeSummary: Cruz owned a Florida DME supplier and, with a co-conspirator, paid kickbacks and bribes to obtain signed doctors' orders that were used to ship thousands of orthotic braces to hundreds of Medicare beneficiaries nationwide who neither requested nor needed them, then billed Medicare $11.4 million; he also falsely told Medicare he was the sole owner to hide his convicted-felon partner, and withdrew proceeds in cash amounts just under the $10,000 bank reporting threshold (structuring).

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida
cases.FraudEntity: Christian "Chris" Cruz (nursing assistant; owner/operator of a Florida durable medical equipment supplier); unnamed co-conspirator (co-owner, convicted felon, charged and at large)
cases.SchemeSummary: Cruz owned a Florida DME supplier and, with a co-conspirator, paid kickbacks and bribes to obtain signed doctors' orders, then shipped orthotic braces to hundreds of Medicare beneficiaries nationwide who neither requested nor needed them and billed Medicare $11.4 million. He also concealed his felon co-owner from Medicare during enrollment and structured cash withdrawals of proceeds just under $10,000 at multiple South Florida bank branches.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of California
cases.FraudEntity: Anar Rustamov (creator/operator of Dublin Helping Hand); Dublin Helping Hand
cases.State_County: California - Alameda County (Dublin); California - Santa Clara County (Sunnyvale)
cases.SchemeSummary: Rustamov allegedly created an entity, Dublin Helping Hand, and submitted thousands of claims to Medicare Advantage Organizations for durable medical equipment such as blood glucose monitors and orthotic braces that was never provided, was not medically necessary, and was not ordered by the referring provider listed on the claims; beneficiaries were unaware their information was used.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of North Carolina
cases.FraudEntity: James Thomas Foley (owner/affiliate of DME supply companies); Randal Fenton Wood (co-defendant, pleaded guilty)
cases.SchemeSummary: Foley and others allegedly bought Medicare beneficiary information and prefilled DME orders from marketing entities that solicited beneficiaries with waived copays/deductibles, then used a 'doctor chase' model to pressure physicians into signing or altering orders for medically unnecessary braces and pneumatic compression devices; DME companies owned by or affiliated with Foley received over $14 million from Medicare alone, with additional billing to CHAMPVA and TRICARE. Co-defendant Randal Fenton Wood previously pleaded guilty in the same conspiracy.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Mexico
cases.FraudEntity: William C. Gardner, DDS (former Albuquerque dentist)
cases.SchemeSummary: After his New Mexico dental license was revoked and his state controlled-substances registration expired, the dentist continued to use his DEA registration number and his office's electronic medical records system to issue 94 prescriptions (mostly Schedule II narcotics); the court found him liable for 80 unlawful prescriptions and imposed a $4,000 civil penalty per violation under the Controlled Substances Act, totaling a $320,000 judgment.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Washington
cases.FraudEntity: Andrew Voegel-Podadera (anesthesiology resident, UW Medicine system)
cases.SchemeSummary: A resident anesthesiologist rotating at Seattle Children's Hospital, Harborview and UW Medical Centers secretly took fentanyl, hydromorphone and other narcotics intended for his patients, refilling the vials with saline and returning them to the pharmacy as 'wastage,' and used the drugs while on duty treating patients; he obtained the controlled substances by fraud and was sentenced to one year of supervised release with 200 hours of community service.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York
cases.FraudEntity: Jean Ronald Tirelus (former chairman of the nonprofit's board of directors); Roberto Samedy (executive director); Edouardo St. Fort (vendor company owner); Miguel Jorge (vendor company owner)
cases.PayerName: Medicaid (New York); New York City (homeless shelter contracts)
cases.SchemeSummary: Tirelus and Samedy, leaders of a Brooklyn nonprofit that provided Medicaid-funded home care and operated NYC homeless shelters, allegedly embezzled more than $1.3 million, including inducing the board in May 2023 to approve an $800,000 'affordable housing joint venture' investment that was wired to a shell company controlled by Tirelus; separately they steered millions in shelter security, maintenance and furniture contracts to vendor companies controlled by St. Fort and Jorge in exchange for bribes and kickbacks.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: Dr. Pankaj Merchia (physician); Dr. Shona Pendse (alleged co-conspirator, charged)
cases.State_County: Massachusetts - Norfolk County (Brookline); Florida - Palm Beach County (Boca Raton)
cases.SchemeSummary: Physician billed former patients' insurance companies from 2017 to 2019 for monthly CPAP/BiPAP machine rentals although he had not treated those patients since at least 2011 and some had returned the devices; separately he billed over $390,000 to another insurer for a CPAP machine supplied to his own brother, and after being told the insurer would not pay for treatment of a family member he created a new medical business and resubmitted the claims. Proceeds funded a Brookline home, a $250,000 wire transfer and at least $140,000 in securities; he also concealed over $6.5 million in medical business income from the IRS through a sham 2008 sale of the businesses to a co-conspirator.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: Dr. Pankaj Merchia (physician); Dr. Shona Pendse (alleged co-conspirator, charged)
cases.State_County: Massachusetts - Norfolk County (Brookline); Florida - Palm Beach County (Boca Raton)
cases.SchemeSummary: Merchia billed former patients' insurers for monthly CPAP/BiPAP machine rentals from 2017-2019 although he had not treated those patients since at least 2011 and some had returned the devices; he separately billed another insurer over $390,000 for a CPAP machine supplied to his brother, creating a new medical business to resubmit claims after being told family-member treatment was not payable. He also concealed over $6.5 million in medical business income from the IRS via a sham 2008 sale of the businesses to a co-conspirator, and used fraud proceeds to buy a Brookline home, wire $250,000 and buy at least $140,000 in securities.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section / National Fraud Enforcement Division
cases.FraudEntity: Renat Abramov (former bank relationship manager, Brooklyn branch)
cases.SchemeSummary: A Russia-based transnational criminal organization submitted fraudulent durable medical equipment claims to Medicare and private insurers through dozens of companies held by nominee owners; Abramov, a bank relationship manager, opened accounts for those nominee owners and facilitated wires, allowing more than $8 million in fraud proceeds to be deposited and moved offshore.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Delaware
cases.FraudEntity: Dr. Shayasta S. Mufti (physician)
cases.SchemeSummary: Physician allegedly ordered medically unnecessary genetic tests costing Medicare thousands of dollars per patient for more than 100 beneficiaries with whom she had no physician-patient relationship, based on brief telemedicine consultations or none at all, and never reviewed or used the results in treatment.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana (prosecuting); U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas (sentencing)
cases.FraudEntity: Carlos A. Lopez (former DOJ Trial Attorney / lead prosecutor); Barrett R. Howell (Dallas criminal defense attorney)
cases.SchemeSummary: During a federal health care fraud investigation in Dallas, the lead DOJ prosecutor (Lopez) and a defense attorney (Howell) each deleted text messages between them from their cell phones after a court ordered production of all their communications; Lopez produced only an incomplete set of screenshots. Both pleaded guilty to misdemeanor unauthorized disposal of government records and were sentenced to probation (1 year for Lopez, 6 months for Howell) with fines totaling $7,500 plus $25 special assessments each.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
cases.FraudEntity: Angela K. Boston, indicted as Angela Williams (former doctor)
cases.SchemeSummary: Boston applied for a position on the medical staff of the Choctaw Nation Health Services Authority in Oklahoma using the stolen identity of a St. Louis physician, submitting forged diplomas in the victim doctor's name and a forged State of Missouri medical license; she had previously used the same doctor's identity to fraudulently obtain controlled substances, writing prescriptions in others' names and using another doctor's prescription pad and DEA number.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division Fraud Section and U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: Sanja Ilic (former Chief Regulatory Officer, ExThera Medical Corporation); ExThera Medical Corporation (medical device manufacturer)
cases.State_County: California - Carlsbad (defendant); Northern California (company); treatments performed at a clinic in Antigua
cases.SchemeSummary: Ilic, ExThera's chief regulatory officer, concealed from the FDA reportable adverse events - including the deaths of at least two cancer patients treated with the company's blood filtration device at a clinic in Antigua - to avoid regulatory scrutiny, loss of clinical trial partners and financial harm after ExThera had secured $10 million and was launching its first U.S. clinical study. Ilic was charged and agreed to plead guilty; ExThera entered a three-year deferred prosecution agreement, agreeing to a $750,000 criminal penalty (placed in escrow) and consenting to a $5,694,750 forfeiture order.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of South Carolina
cases.FraudEntity: Kevin S. Murdock (owner/CEO of Premier Medical Laboratory Services); Thomas C. Lee (high-level employee); Vidhya V. Narayanan (high-level employee); Premier Medical Laboratory Services
cases.SchemeSummary: Defendants at a Greenville diagnostic lab allegedly billed federal health care programs for individual COVID-19 tests when the specimens had actually been pooled together for faster combined processing, and manipulated test processing software, so that the billed tests were virtually worthless and ineligible for reimbursement. Murdock separately agreed to a $27,544,460 consent judgment in a related False Claims Act civil action brought by the U.S. and Colorado, Georgia and South Carolina.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Alabama
cases.FraudEntity: Hasan Jermel Pulliam (child and family therapist, enrolled Alabama Medicaid provider)
cases.SchemeSummary: Pulliam, a child and family therapist enrolled with Alabama Medicaid in October 2018, used beneficiary identifying information (names, DOBs, Medicaid Recipient ID numbers) obtained through provider referrals, without patient or family consent, to submit claims for counseling sessions that were never provided, receiving $718,967.20 in Medicaid payments through November 2023.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
cases.FraudEntity: Florence Ndubizu (co-owner and pharmacist-in-charge, Healthcare Pharmacy); Healthcare Pharmacy
cases.SchemeSummary: As co-owner and pharmacist-in-charge of a single-location Trenton pharmacy, Ndubizu and employees filled fraudulent oxycodone prescriptions outside the usual course of professional practice, dispensing millions of dosage units (over 800,000 pills in 2014, 900,000 in 2015, 800,000 in 2016, 200,000 in 2017) that were diverted to street-level dealers, and she manipulated pharmacy records to evade state and federal reporting; a DEA audit found more than 64,000 oxycodone pills diverted between April 2015 and August 2017.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of South Carolina
cases.FraudEntity: Jerome Sydney Heyward (former North Charleston City Councilmember); Mike A. Brown (former North Charleston City Council Member); Michelle Stent-Hilton (non-profit applicant); Donavan Laval Moten (founder, Core4Success Foundation); Aaron Charles-Lee Hicks (bribe payer); Hason Fields; Rose Lorenzo (money laundering co-conspirator)
cases.SchemeSummary: Public corruption, not health care fraud: North Charleston Councilman Heyward extorted a businessman for payments tied to official action, took bribes with Councilman Brown from Aaron Hicks to support a rezoning of the Baker Hospital site, and accepted $20,000 kickbacks each from Moten and Stent-Hilton in exchange for supporting their non-profits' applications for city violence-reduction grant funds, then laundered the proceeds with Rose Lorenzo. Heyward received 72 months and $200,000 restitution; Brown 24 months; Stent-Hilton and Moten 18 months each; Hicks previously 15 months.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: David Fuhrmann (former Northeast regional national sales director for a mobile medical diagnostics company)
cases.SchemeSummary: Fuhrmann and co-conspirators at a mobile diagnostics company paid doctors cash and checks per transcranial doppler (TCD) brain ultrasound ordered, disguising the per-test payments as fair-market-value space rental and administrative services agreements; the medically unnecessary scans generated about $70.6 million in Medicare billings, of which Medicare paid roughly $27.2 million.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section (federal jury in Dallas)
cases.FraudEntity: Keith J. Gray (owner and operator of Axis Professional Labs LLC and Kingdom Health Laboratory LLC); Axis Professional Labs LLC; Kingdom Health Laboratory LLC
cases.SchemeSummary: Gray's two clinical labs billed Medicare approximately $328 million (about $54 million paid) for medically unnecessary cardiovascular genetic tests obtained by paying per-sample kickbacks to marketers who used telemarketing and 'doctor chase' tactics to secure beneficiary DNA samples, Medicare numbers and signed physician test orders; kickbacks were disguised as 'marketing' hours, 'software' payments and fictitious loans, and proceeds were laundered through luxury vehicle purchases.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Florida
cases.FraudEntity: Joel Rufus French (owner of a marketing company and of eight durable medical equipment supply companies; former NFL player)
cases.State_County: Florida - Orange County (Orlando); Mississippi - Monroe County (Amory)
cases.PayerName: Medicare; CHAMPVA (Civilian Health and Medical Program of the Department of Veterans Affairs)
cases.SchemeSummary: French used overseas call centers to pressure elderly Medicare beneficiaries (including Alzheimer's and dementia patients, with some call recordings altered to fake consent) into accepting medically unnecessary orthotic braces, then paid sham telemedicine companies for doctor and nurse practitioner orders signed without any examination; he sold those orders to marketers and DME suppliers and also billed Medicare and CHAMPVA directly through eight DME companies he concealed his ownership of with false documents, including claims for braces for amputees' missing limbs and for deceased beneficiaries, and paid cash (about $225,000 withdrawn, over $10,000 hand-delivered to Orlando) for beneficiary information.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section (Office of Public Affairs); National Fraud Enforcement Division
cases.FraudEntity: Joel Rufus French (owner of a marketing company and beneficial owner of eight durable medical equipment companies)
cases.State_County: Mississippi - Armory (Monroe County); Florida - Orange County (Orlando)
cases.PayerName: Medicare; CHAMPVA (Civilian Health and Medical Program of the Department of Veterans Affairs)
cases.SchemeSummary: French used overseas telemarketing call centers to pressure elderly Medicare beneficiaries and CHAMPVA families into accepting medically unnecessary orthotic braces (sometimes altering call recordings to fake consent), paid kickbacks to sham telemedicine companies for doctors' orders signed by clinicians who never examined the patients, sold those orders to marketers/DME suppliers, and also billed Medicare and CHAMPVA directly through eight DME companies he concealed behind straw owners and false documents; he laundered roughly $225,000 in cash, including over $10,000 driven to Orlando to pay accomplices selling beneficiary data.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: Ariana Foley (nurse)
cases.SchemeSummary: While working an overnight ICU shift at a Boston-area hospital, the nurse checked out a bag of Versed (a benzodiazepine) and three bags of fentanyl assigned to an intubated, immobile patient, none of which were scanned into the patient's medical record; she was found slumped in the patient's room with three syringes in her pocket. She pleaded guilty to unlawfully obtaining controlled substances by fraud, deception and subterfuge and received three years' probation and 100 hours of community service.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
cases.FraudEntity: Adam Brosius (director of business development, later president of Main Avenue Pharmacy); Main Avenue Pharmacy
cases.SchemeSummary: Main Avenue Pharmacy, a mail-order pharmacy, identified compounded drug formulas (scar creams, pain creams, migraine medication, vitamins) with high reimbursement, printed pre-formulated prescription pads and distributed them through marketers to telemedicine companies and doctors; after billing Medicare, TRICARE and commercial payers roughly $33 million for these medically unnecessary compounds, it paid the marketers kickbacks based on referral volume and reimbursement received. Brosius was ordered to pay $33 million restitution and $27 million forfeiture.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Pennsylvania
cases.FraudEntity: Mark Marriott (former facilities manager, Primary Health Network); Drew Pierce (former CEO, Primary Health Network); Jack Laeng (former CEO, Primary Health Network); TopCoat (shell vendor company)
cases.SchemeSummary: Executives and a facilities manager of non-profit Primary Health Network inserted a sham company, TopCoat, made up of PHN insiders, between PHN and its legitimate vendors; PHN paid TopCoat inflated amounts while TopCoat did no work and paid the real vendors less, causing over $500,000 in loss. Marriott also directed a PHN vendor to submit inflated invoices to fund kickbacks to himself, Pierce and their jointly owned company, used PHN funds for personal expenses, and failed to report the proceeds on his tax returns. Sentences span three defendants: Pierce 40 months, Marriott 30 months, Laeng 24 months.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Kentucky
cases.FraudEntity: Delores Jordan (owner of Serenity Keeper's, LLC); Ernest Williams (operator of sober homes); Serenity Keeper's, LLC (sober home company); Jerome Davis (co-defendant, owner of X-Tremly for Christ, LLC); Dashawn Dawkins (co-defendant); Lily Bell (paid the kickbacks)
cases.SchemeSummary: Jordan, owner of the Serenity Keepers sober home company, solicited and received kickbacks (checks, cash, ACH/'consulting' payments of up to $5,000 routed through co-defendant Davis's company) in exchange for referring residents' urine drug testing to three labs, causing Medicare and Medicaid to pay those labs about $2,569,946 for tests that were not ordered or reviewed by a medical provider and were done for non-medical reasons; Serenity Keepers also billed Medicaid for six hours per day of peer support services that were not actually provided and were not delivered by licensed peer support specialists, with Williams receiving $365,374.72 as a percentage of the billings. Jordan received 60 months, Williams five years' probation, and co-defendant Davis 12 months and a day.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
cases.FraudEntity: Craig A. Spiegel (pediatrician); April Bingham (co-defendant/patient)
cases.SchemeSummary: A pediatrician prescribed controlled substances to at least 19 patients in exchange for cash, sex acts or nude photos, including writing prescriptions for his co-defendant under the names of her friends and relatives to exploit their insurance benefits; the medically unnecessary prescriptions caused $114,480 in losses to Medicare, Missouri Medicaid and Illinois Medicaid. Spiegel received 20 years and was ordered to repay $114,480; co-defendant Bingham received 21 months.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of California
cases.FraudEntity: Jeanett Valenzuela Ayub (owner/operator of durable medical equipment companies); Fernando Valenzuela Ayub (co-conspirator, brother); multiple DME companies; sham marketing companies
cases.State_County: California - San Diego County (Chula Vista/San Diego)
cases.SchemeSummary: Defendant and co-conspirators owned durable medical equipment companies that billed Medicare nearly $51 million (about $20 million paid) for orthotic braces supported by bogus prescriptions purchased through $3.7 million in kickbacks to sham marketing companies; the prescribing physicians never examined or spoke with the beneficiaries, many of whom never opened the delivered braces. When companies were suspended from Medicare billing, new DME companies were placed in nominee owners' names while the conspirators retained control, and at least $14 million of Medicare proceeds was laundered. Figures cover the conspiracy involving Jeanett Valenzuela Ayub and her brother Fernando, who pleaded guilty earlier and awaits sentencing.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
cases.FraudEntity: Michael W. Luehrsen
cases.SchemeSummary: Luehrsen, previously tried for conspiring to commit health care fraud involving an altered compound prescription form faxed from his father's Western New York home in June/July 2014, falsely testified under oath in February 2022 that he was out of town on the dates the prescriptions were faxed; cell phone photos, phone and financial records showed he was in Buffalo. He was convicted of perjury and sentenced to three years' probation, roughly $2,000,000 restitution and roughly $2,000,000 forfeiture.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Rhode Island
cases.FraudEntity: Thomas Sandgaard (former CEO, Zynex, Inc.); Anna Lucsok (former COO, Zynex, Inc.); Zynex, Inc. (medical device company)
cases.State_County: Colorado (Castle Rock and Denver); prosecuted in Rhode Island
cases.PayerName: Government and private health care payors (not specifically named; investigated by HHS-OIG, DoD/DCIS, VA-OIG, OPM-OIG)
cases.SchemeSummary: Indictment alleges the CEO and COO of Zynex caused the company to ship and bill for electrotherapy device supplies (electrodes, batteries) in excessive volumes - up to 32, 64 or 128 electrode pairs per patient per month - that were not medically necessary, not covered, and not requested by patients, collecting over $873 million (including $600 million for supplies) from government and private payors and billing patients directly; the inflated billings were then used to overstate Zynex revenues and drive up its stock price, adding securities and mail fraud counts.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
cases.FraudEntity: E. Bruce DiDonato (founder and former CEO of Campus Eye Management Holdings, LLC); Campus Eye LLC; Campus Eye Surgery Center LLC; Campus Eye Management Holdings, LLC; Campus Eye Management, LLC
cases.SchemeSummary: DiDonato allegedly paid ophthalmologists disguised 'consulting fee' kickbacks - monthly flat fees actually calculated as a percentage of prior-year Medicare reimbursements for diagnostic tests on their referrals - to steer eye surgery patients to his optometry practice and ambulatory surgery center, where they received duplicative or medically unnecessary pre-surgical diagnostic tests that no one reviewed, generating roughly $3.4 million in Medicare claims and about $1 million paid; the Campus Eye entities received a declination and agreed to pay $1 million in disgorgement.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Pennsylvania
cases.FraudEntity: Aaron Hertel (founder/owner); Michael Brown (founder/owner); Hertel & Brown Physical and Aquatic Therapy (company); 18 additional co-defendant employees
cases.PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid (Pennsylvania); TRICARE; Department of Veterans Affairs health programs; Federal Employees Health Benefits (OPM); private health insurers
cases.SchemeSummary: The owners of a five-location physical therapy practice used unlicensed technicians to treat patients but billed insurers as though licensed physical therapists and assistants had provided the care; they also billed more treatment time per day than the clinics were open and altered patient schedules to make group treatment appear as the one-on-one therapy Medicare requires. Both owners each received 72 months and a $250,000 fine (total $500,000 in fines); restitution from them and the company is to be set at an April hearing.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Nebraska
cases.FraudEntity: Angie Albert; Brent Conaway; Phyllis M. Rooney; Cassi Wigington
cases.State_County: Nebraska (District of Nebraska); Nebraska - Douglas County (Omaha)
cases.PayerName: Medicare; Nebraska Medicaid; other unnamed insurers
cases.SchemeSummary: Four separate Nebraska-district defendants charged in the 2026 national takedown: Albert and Conaway allegedly submitted approximately $4,451,498 in false Medicare and Medicaid claims for Spravato (ketamine nasal spray) treatments not rendered and overcharged for the medication, receiving about $976,979 in overpayments (vehicles, a motorcycle, an RV and their residence subject to forfeiture); Rooney allegedly made false statements billing Nebraska Medicaid $92,582 for mental health counseling she did not provide; and Wigington allegedly billed Nebraska Medicaid and other insurers $445,455 for custom-made breast prostheses patients never received. Figures span multiple defendants.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Hampshire
cases.FraudEntity: Fructoso de Jesus Gomez Agudelo, a/k/a Jesus Gomez (individual, identity theft to obtain benefits); Kakha Bendeliani (nominee owner, Centennial Med Supply LLC); Goga Danelia (assisted nominee owner); Centennial Med Supply LLC (DME company); Rima Gerges-Maalouf (per diem pharmacist)
cases.State_County: New Hampshire - Nashua (Hillsborough County); New Hampshire - northern New Hampshire (pharmacy)
cases.SchemeSummary: Four separate New Hampshire cases in the 2026 national takedown: Bendeliani and Danelia allegedly laundered proceeds of a nationwide scheme that billed Medicare nearly $3 billion for medically unnecessary durable medical equipment (mostly urinary catheters) not provided as represented, with about $12.6 million paid to shell DME company Centennial Med Supply and roughly $13 million withdrawn as cashier's checks, redeposited and wired overseas; Gomez Agudelo allegedly used a stolen U.S. citizen's identity for over 20 years to obtain more than $500,000 in Medicare, Medicaid, Social Security, housing and SNAP benefits; and pharmacist Gerges-Maalouf allegedly diverted about 147 patient pills/capsules of controlled substances in August 2024.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
cases.FraudEntity: Pan American Inc. (pharmacy); St. Mina and St. Moses Pharmacy d/b/a Well Care Pharmacy; Farmacia Latina Corp.; Perfect Care Pharmacy LLC
cases.State_County: New Jersey - Hudson County (West New York, Bayonne, Union City, Jersey City)
cases.PayerName: Medicare Part D; New Jersey Medicaid
cases.SchemeSummary: Four Hudson County pharmacies billed Medicare Part D (and, for Pan American, New Jersey Medicaid) for prescription drugs never dispensed to beneficiaries; wholesaler inventory records showed they had not purchased enough medication to fill the prescriptions billed. Settlement amounts across the four defendants total $4,325,000 ($3.1M Pan American, $490,000 Well Care, $375,000 Farmacia Latina, $360,000 Perfect Care).

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Minnesota; U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
cases.FraudEntity: Moktar Hassan Aden; Mustafa Dayib Ali; Khalid Ahmed Dayib; Abdifitah Mohamud Mohamed; Brilliant Minds Services LLC (Medicaid-enrolled provider operated by the four defendants)
cases.PayerName: Medicaid (Minnesota Medicaid - Housing Stabilization Services program)
cases.SchemeSummary: Four men enrolled Brilliant Minds Services LLC as a Minnesota Medicaid provider in the Griggs-Midway Building, signed up roughly 350 disabled/homeless Medicaid recipients for Housing Stabilization Services, then billed thousands of claims for services never provided or inflated, taking about $2.2 million; when insurers requested supporting documentation, they used ChatGPT to fabricate records. All four pleaded guilty to one count of wire fraud each; sentencing not yet set.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, National Fraud Enforcement Division; U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Ohio; U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Ohio; Ohio Attorney General's Medicaid Fraud Control Unit (Butler County Common Pleas Court)
cases.FraudEntity: Four unnamed defendants (owners/operators of behavioral health services organizations, Southern District of Ohio); Robert Haley, 63, of Cincinnati (Butler County behavioral health billing); four unnamed defendants (PPP loan applicants, Southern District of Ohio); Jamal Abubakari; Kamal Abubakari; Amanda Joy Opoku-Boachie; Frederick Kumi; Daniel Yussif (romance scam defendants)
cases.State_County: Ohio - Butler County; Ohio - Hamilton County (Cincinnati); Ohio (Southern and Northern Districts)
cases.PayerName: Medicaid (Ohio Medicaid); Small Business Administration (Paycheck Protection Program)
cases.SchemeSummary: In a coordinated federal-state takedown, nine defendants were charged with over $42 million in fraud: four defendants allegedly ran behavioral health organizations that billed Ohio Medicaid over $30 million for therapeutic behavioral services and psychotherapy purportedly delivered to children at summer camps, church groups and recreational programs, where services were medically unnecessary or not provided as represented, and continued billing through a different entity after one company lost its credentialing with the Ohio Department of Mental Health and Addiction Services; separately, Robert Haley was indicted in Butler County for over $12 million in Medicaid billing for therapeutic behavioral services never provided to children in after-school programs. The document also covers a $1.4 million PPP loan fraud (falsified 1040 Schedule C income) and a $15 million romance scam; agents seized three bank accounts holding $469,000 and 14 luxury vehicles worth $800,000 in the behavioral health case.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, National Fraud Enforcement Division; U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida
cases.FraudEntity: Unnamed founder and owner of HealthSplash
cases.PayerName: Medicare; other federal health care benefit programs
cases.SchemeSummary: A federal jury in the Southern District of Florida convicted the founder/owner of HealthSplash for running a platform that generated false doctors' orders and prescriptions, which were used to bill Medicare and other federal health care programs more than $1 billion for medically unnecessary equipment. (The same DOJ roundup also noted an unrelated indictment of a podiatrist and two nurses over $29 million in Medicare-paid skin substitute claims.)

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, National Fraud Enforcement Division; U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
cases.FraudEntity: E. Bruce DiDonato (founder of optometry practice and ambulatory surgery center; CEO of Campus Eye); Campus Eye Management Holdings LLC; Campus Eye Management LLC (management services organization)
cases.SchemeSummary: DiDonato allegedly paid ophthalmologists disguised 'consulting fee' kickbacks - monthly flat fees actually calculated as a percentage of the prior year's Medicare reimbursements for tests on their referred patients - to refer surgery patients, who were then subjected to duplicative or medically unnecessary diagnostic eye tests that no one reviewed, generating roughly $3.4 million in claims to Medicare of which about $1 million was paid; the management company Campus Eye self-disclosed, received a declination, and agreed to repay $1 million to victims.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Minnesota; Criminal Division Fraud Section
cases.FraudEntity: Anthony Waddell Jefferson (business owner/HSS provider); Lester Brown (business owner/HSS provider)
cases.SchemeSummary: Two Philadelphia men enrolled businesses in Minneapolis as providers in Minnesota's Medicaid-funded Housing Stabilization Services program, recruited roughly 230 Medicaid beneficiaries at homeless shelters and Section 8 housing, signed them up, and billed for housing-support services never provided; when insurers requested documentation they fabricated emails and used ChatGPT to generate fake client notes, obtaining about $3.5 million.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division, Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Arkansas
cases.FraudEntity: Atlanta Gastroenterology Associates (gastroenterology practice); Advanced Pathology Solutions (APS) (pathology laboratory)
cases.State_County: Georgia - Fulton County (Atlanta); Arkansas - Pulaski County (Little Rock)
cases.SchemeSummary: APS built and supported an in-house limited-capacity pathology lab inside Atlanta Gastroenterology Associates' office, providing benefits alleged to be unlawful remuneration in exchange for exclusive referral of gastrointestinal pathology specimens; the practice billed Medicare and other insurers for the technical component while APS billed the professional component. The practice also billed for medically unnecessary special stains ordered on a blanket/reflex basis without pathologist review of a routine stain or medical-record justification.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
cases.FraudEntity: Steven D. Peyroux (chiropractor)
cases.State_County: Georgia - Canton (defendant's residence); scheme conducted nationwide
cases.SchemeSummary: Peyroux and co-conspirators paid and received kickbacks for nationwide Medicare beneficiary information (names, Medicare ID numbers) and fabricated audio recordings of people posing as beneficiaries requesting over-the-counter COVID-19 tests, then billed Medicare millions for OTC COVID-19 tests that were never requested or eligible; they recruited additional providers to bill under sham agreements and made false statements in response to Medicare audits to conceal the scheme. He agreed to over $6.5 million in restitution.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs (Criminal Division Fraud Section / National Fraud Enforcement Division)
cases.FraudEntity: Irakli Nakashidze (owner of ABRH Care Inc.); ABRH Care Inc. (sham medical supply company)
cases.SchemeSummary: ABRH Care Inc., a sham Miami medical supply company owned by Nakashidze, billed Medicare and private insurers roughly $179 million in the first half of 2025 for orthotic braces and wound dressings never provided to patients, as part of a transnational criminal organization's scheme; Nakashidze laundered over $1.1 million of the proceeds to co-conspirators, including wire transfers to accounts in China and Hong Kong, and was ordered to forfeit $1,108,504.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of West Virginia
cases.FraudEntity: MWI Veterinary Supply Inc., also known as MWI Animal Health (DEA-registered veterinary drug distributor); Dr. Clara Ann Mason (Putnam County veterinarian)
cases.State_County: West Virginia - Putnam County; Idaho - Boise (distributor headquarters)
cases.FraudType: Controlled substance diversion / suspicious order reporting failure
FraudTypeAll: Controlled substance diversion / suspicious order reporting failure
cases.SchemeSummary: MWI, a DEA-registered veterinary drug distributor, filled repeated large opioid orders (14,200 hydrocodone/acetaminophen 10mg units and 1,400 oxycodone HCl units) from a single West Virginia veterinarian between March 2018 and July 2023 without investigating or reporting them as suspicious to DEA, including releasing a flagged 300-unit oxycodone order after one day with no substantial review; MWI paid $100,000 to resolve Controlled Substances Act allegations, while the veterinarian, Dr. Clara Ann Mason, had a separate $956,709 default civil penalty judgment entered against her for unsecured, untracked opioids and apparently fabricated records.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Tennessee
cases.FraudEntity: Angela Moss (physician, owner and operator of Gordonsville Clinic)
cases.SchemeSummary: Indictment alleges the physician, who owned and operated Gordonsville Clinic, prescribed medically unnecessary controlled substances - more than 5.6 million pills and doses over eight years - without a legitimate medical purpose, and billed health care programs for the associated care; charged with seven counts of health care fraud and twelve counts of unauthorized distribution of controlled substances.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of South Carolina
cases.FraudEntity: Jonathan Wade Sumter (ringleader); Jason Elijah Sumter; Gerothia McCullough
cases.PayerName: U.S. Small Business Administration (Paycheck Protection Program and Economic Injury Disaster Loan programs)
cases.SchemeSummary: Three defendants applied for PPP and EIDL pandemic relief funds on behalf of six sham or defunct companies (Living Water Outreach, High Consulting, Lyons Transport, GSM Home Care, Challenge Consulting, Omni Holdings), submitting fabricated company expenses, employee wage statements and other false documents to obtain over $1.8 million, which they split. Jonathan Sumter received 80 months (concurrent with a 92-month sentence from a 2023 health care fraud conviction) and $1,802,741 restitution; Jason Sumter 36 months and $739,786; McCullough 12 months and $478,366 plus vehicle forfeiture.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of North Carolina
cases.FraudEntity: Gwendolyn Singleton (owner/operator of Joelle's Center of Hope); Joelle's Center of Hope
cases.SchemeSummary: Singleton, through her purported substance abuse treatment business Joelle's Center of Hope, billed North Carolina Medicaid directly for approximately $1,735,865 in urine drug tests that were never performed, listing a nurse practitioner and a doctor as ordering providers though neither had ordered any tests; Medicaid reimbursed over $1.7 million.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. District Court for the District of Vermont; Justice Department Criminal Division, Fraud Section
cases.FraudEntity: Evelyn Herrera (owner, Merida Medical Supplies Inc.); Merida Medical Supplies Inc. (durable medical equipment company)
cases.SchemeSummary: Herrera, through her DME company Merida, obtained the identities of individuals in Vermont, New England and elsewhere and submitted roughly $6.5 million in Medicare claims for wrist, knee and back braces that patients never requested or received, collecting about $2.8 million; she pleaded guilty to conspiracy to pay health care kickbacks and laundered proceeds by moving over $300,000 to a cryptocurrency exchange, wiring $125,000 abroad for property in Tulum, Mexico, and withdrawing cash after CMS suspended payments.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
cases.FraudEntity: Christina Mareik a.k.a. Christina Marie Sanchez Hernandez (prescription facilitator); Paul Richard Randall (patient marketer, Monte VP LLC dba Monte Vista Pharmacy); Kyrollos Mekail (owner, Monte Vista Pharmacy); Patricia Anderson (prescriber who signed prescriptions); Oren David Shachar (owner of Gentle Touch Hospice Care Inc., Oxford Hospice Care Inc., Art of Hospice Inc., Holly Trinity Hospice); Abraham Shin (marketer); Jeannie Choi (marketer); Brenda Lee Lopez (medical office manager); Lynn Galbraith (owner, Azure Hospice Care Inc.); Dr. Eugene Richard Dorsey (psychiatrist, Western Orthopaedic Surgical Associates); Wisam Khader (physician); Patrick Murphy (physician); Justin Evans (physician)
cases.State_County: California - Los Angeles County (Whittier, West Hills, Van Nuys, Valley Glen, Encino, Glendale, Torrance, Norwalk); California - Orange County (Orange, Irvine, Anaheim, Garden Grove, Santa Ana); California - San Bernardino County (Montclair); California - Riverside County (Moreno Valley)
cases.PayerName: Medi-Cal (California Medicaid); Medicare; U.S. Department of Labor Office of Workers' Compensation Programs
cases.SchemeSummary: Consolidated Central District of California takedown covering 10 defendants in separate schemes: Mareik and co-schemers at Monte Vista Pharmacy created and had a nurse/provider sign prescriptions for patients she never saw, exploiting Medi-Cal's suspended prior-authorization rules to bill nearly $270M (over $178M paid) for 19 high-cost non-contracted drugs with cheap generic ingredients, many never delivered, then fabricated progress notes to survive a state audit; Shachar's four hospice companies billed Medicare ~$27M for hospice care for patients who were not terminally ill or already deceased, using identities bought from marketers Shin and Choi and paying kickbacks to marketers and beneficiaries; office manager Lopez forged four providers' signatures on orders for UTI, respiratory panel and toxicology tests for beneficiaries who gave no specimens (some deceased), causing a lab to bill Medicare ~$9.09M and paying her ~$335,000 in referral kickbacks; Galbraith billed Medicare ~$2.27M in fraudulent hospice claims; and psychiatrist Dorsey falsified psychiatric reports to qualify claimants for federal workers' compensation, causing ~$1.83M in overpayments. Figures span multiple defendants and separate cases.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maryland
cases.FraudEntity: CVR Management, LLC (health care management company); Center for Vein Restoration; Center for Vascular Medicine (CVM), LLC; Sanjiv Lakhanpal, MD, FACS (CEO, president, and CVM chairman of the board)
cases.State_County: Maryland - Greenbelt (Prince George's County); Maryland; Virginia; North Carolina
cases.PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid (eight states and the District of Columbia); TRICARE
cases.SchemeSummary: Over a six-year period the vein-treatment practices billed Medicare, Medicaid and TRICARE for sclerotherapy, radiofrequency ablation and endovenous laser ablation for chronic venous insufficiency that were not clinically indicated and medically unnecessary, including treatment that was essentially cosmetic and performed without the required prior period of unsuccessful conservative therapy. Resolved by a $4 million FCA settlement (federal share $3,395,634.93; Medicaid recovery $604,365.07) arising from two qui tam suits by former employees, whose relators' share is $752,000.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
cases.FraudEntity: Michael Kochen (owner of durable medical equipment companies); Sandro Herek (telemarketing company owner directing overseas call centers)
cases.State_County: Florida - Miami-Dade County (Miami); Florida - Broward County (Coral Springs); Florida - Miami-Dade County (Aventura)
cases.SchemeSummary: Kochen owned dozens of DME companies and paid kickbacks to Herek, who ran overseas call centers (Egypt and elsewhere) that cold-called and high-pressured elderly Medicare Advantage beneficiaries into accepting back, knee, shoulder and ankle braces; Kochen also paid kickbacks to telemedicine companies whose physicians issued boilerplate brace authorizations based only on call recordings, often without speaking to the beneficiary, supporting roughly $35 million in claims and over $19 million in payments. Both defendants were convicted at trial and sentenced (204 and 92 months).

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Texas
cases.FraudEntity: Mouzon Bass, III (sole owner and president of Vivature); Lance Wilson (senior executive at Vivature); Vivature (healthcare billing company)
cases.SchemeSummary: Bass, owner/president of healthcare billing company Vivature, and Wilson, a senior Vivature executive, pleaded guilty to wire fraud conspiracies involving COVID-19 testing and an athletic training billing scheme; the document does not detail the billing mechanics or amounts.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of California
cases.FraudEntity: Neery Velazquez (healthcare worker employed by a government contractor at CBP detention facilities)
cases.PayerName: U.S. Customs and Border Protection (federal government contractor travel reimbursement)
cases.SchemeSummary: Velazquez, a contractor healthcare worker at CBP detention facilities, kept claiming Temporary Duty travel reimbursement for lodging, meals and incidental expenses after moving his permanent residence to San Diego, submitting about 35 monthly travel claims with false attestations plus a forged month-to-month lease and rental receipt from a fictitious landlord to inflate claimed rent; he submitted roughly $244,019 in false claims, of which CBP paid about $181,083. The broader investigation found about a third of the contractor's 100 TDY employees in San Diego submitted over $1.59 million in false travel claims.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Indiana
cases.FraudEntity: Bethany A. Cataldi, D.O. (physician, sole owner of the Center for Otolaryngology and Facial Plastic Surgery)
cases.SchemeSummary: Cataldi, sole owner of an otolaryngology practice, billed Medicare and private insurers approximately $50 million for thousands of balloon sinuplasty procedures that were never performed, collecting nearly $20 million, including about $460,000 in co-insurance payments from individual patients; proceeds were used to buy real estate and luxury assets.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
cases.FraudEntity: Camille S. Childress (operator/owner of Inspiring Angels LLC); Inspiring Angels LLC (home health care company)
cases.SchemeSummary: Childress enrolled her home health company with Missouri Medicaid using paperwork falsely naming another person as owner to conceal her ownership after a 2012 criminal conviction, then billed Medicaid for in-home services never provided - including for clients who were hospitalized at the time and for visits with no timesheets or documentation - collecting at least $174,496 in 2021-2022. A related release notes she was later sentenced to 15 months and ordered to repay $174,496.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
cases.FraudEntity: Camille S. Childress (operator/owner of Inspiring Angels LLC); Inspiring Angels LLC (home health care company)
cases.SchemeSummary: Childress submitted false enrollment paperwork claiming someone else owned her home health company, Inspiring Angels LLC, to hide her 2012 disqualifying conviction, then billed Missouri Medicaid $174,496 for home health services never provided - including for clients who were hospitalized at the time and for visits with no timesheets or documentation.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
cases.FraudEntity: Bun Khath (organizer/director of scheme; opened shell companies and bank accounts); Hugo Villanueva (co-defendant, charged)
cases.SchemeSummary: Khath and co-conspirators, including bankers, tax preparers and borrowers, obtained more than $60 million in bank loans by submitting loan applications with fabricated equipment sales invoices, income tax returns and financial/bank statements; Khath opened shell companies and bank accounts to collect the proceeds and wired the funds to coconspirator accounts. At sentencing the court also heard evidence of alleged Medicare fraud he committed while released on bond.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
cases.FraudEntity: John Stevenson Bynon Jr. (physician, Director of Abdominal Organ Transplantation and Surgical Director for Liver Transplantation, Memorial Hermann Health System's Texas Medical Center)
cases.SchemeSummary: Transplant surgeon allegedly entered false statements in the medical records of patients on the UNOS liver transplant waitlist, rendering them functionally ineligible to receive donor organ offers without their knowledge; patients continued receiving care, items and services that Medicare paid for as if they remained eligible. Charged with five counts of making false statements in health care matters.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
cases.FraudEntity: Dr. Feliciano Serrano (physician); Serrano Kidney & Vascular Access Center (medical practice)
cases.SchemeSummary: Physician billed Medicare and California Medicaid for medically unnecessary vascular interventional procedures on 20 beneficiaries - routine, repeated dialysis access angioplasty/stent procedures and peripheral artery disease stent/atherectomy procedures on patients with mild or no stenosis (one patient got ~42 stents, another ~16 atherectomies) - overstating stenosis and falsely documenting symptoms and conservative therapy in medical records to make the claims appear justified. Settlement of $6.73 million total: ~$6.51 million to the United States and ~$229,000 to California, resolving a qui tam action by Lincoln Analytics, Inc. (relator share ~$976,000).

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
cases.FraudEntity: Ana Silvia Garcia (Mexican national illegally residing in Houston; benefits recipient)
cases.SchemeSummary: Beginning in 1992, Garcia used a U.S. citizen's Social Security number to assume that identity, filing immigration petitions for family members and enrolling for disability and Medicare benefits; using the stolen identity she unlawfully collected more than $278,000 in benefits she was not entitled to between 2013 and February 2026.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: Juan Felipe Chalas (Dominican national unlawfully residing in Salem, N.H.)
cases.PayerName: MassHealth (Massachusetts Medicaid); Social Security Administration (disability benefits); USDA SNAP (Massachusetts Department of Transitional Assistance)
cases.SchemeSummary: Defendant, a Dominican national never admitted to the U.S., assumed the identity of a U.S. citizen from Puerto Rico beginning in 1996, using it to obtain U.S. passports (1998, 2010, 2023) and Massachusetts RMV identifications, and to fraudulently enroll in and collect federally funded benefits - $12,584 in SNAP, $25,491 in SSA disability and $266,857 in MassHealth benefits. Plea agreement calls for one year of incarceration (not yet imposed) plus restitution totaling $304,932.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: Amaurys Arias Arias (beneficiary/applicant)
cases.SchemeSummary: Defendant allegedly used a U.S. citizen's stolen identity and falsely represented, including in a sworn affidavit, that he was a U.S. citizen when applying for Massachusetts healthcare benefits, thereby obtaining tens of thousands of dollars in MassHealth benefits for which he was ineligible.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: Manuel Antonio Baez (benefit recipient/applicant)
cases.SchemeSummary: Defendant, a Dominican national unlawfully in the U.S., allegedly used a U.S. citizen's stolen identity and Social Security number, and submitted a sworn affidavit falsely claiming U.S. citizenship, to qualify for and obtain over $80,000 in MassHealth (Massachusetts Medicaid) benefits.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
cases.FraudEntity: Ana Silvia Garcia (Mexican national illegally residing in Houston; benefits recipient)
cases.SchemeSummary: Beginning in 1992, Garcia used a U.S. citizen's Social Security number to assume that identity, filing immigration petitions for family members and enrolling for federal disability and Medicare benefits she was not entitled to, collecting more than $278,000 in benefit payments from 2013 through February 2026.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: Dr. Alexandria Williams (physician); Integrated Support Plus, Inc. (telemedicine company)
cases.SchemeSummary: Dr. Williams signed pre-populated DME orders generated from telemarketing calls to Medicare beneficiaries, falsely attesting she had evaluated the patients and discussed orthotics use; the signed orders enabled DME suppliers to bill Medicare for medically unnecessary orthotic braces, and she was paid per order reviewed via a staffing company linked to telemedicine firm Integrated Support Plus, Inc.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Wisconsin
cases.FraudEntity: George Dilles (president and part-owner of NG Enterprises, Inc., d.b.a. Visiting Angels); NG Enterprises, Inc. (d.b.a. Visiting Angels)
cases.SchemeSummary: The president and part-owner of an elderly home personal care agency withheld federal income, Social Security and Medicare taxes from employees' wages but willfully failed to file Forms 941 or pay over more than $1.2 million to the IRS for 17 quarters, spending funds on personal expenses including mortgage payments and a Maserati and McLaren; he also used unfiled employment tax returns to obtain a $312,500 Paycheck Protection Program loan.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: Kartik Bhatia (owner/operator of DME company); Raju Sharma (co-conspirator)
cases.SchemeSummary: Bhatia and co-conspirators owned and operated DME companies that paid telemarketing firms for orders for orthotic braces (ankle, wrist, knee, back), then billed Medicare over $2 million; beneficiaries often did not need or want the braces and the physicians whose signatures appeared on the orders never treated or prescribed for them. After CMS suspended payments to his first DME company, Bhatia opened a new one and continued the same conduct.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice — National Fraud Enforcement Division
cases.FraudEntity: Unnamed New York man (money launderer for pharmacy fraud scheme); unnamed Florida man (participant in $33 million health care fraud and kickback scheme in Newark, New Jersey); unnamed Detroit surgeon; unnamed Missouri medical doctor; unnamed Dominican national residing in Brockton, Massachusetts
cases.State_County: New York; New Jersey - Essex County (Newark); Michigan - Wayne County (Detroit); Missouri; Massachusetts - Plymouth County (Brockton)
cases.SchemeSummary: Weekly DOJ enforcement roundup covering several separate health care matters: a New York man received 5 years for laundering proceeds of a $24.4 million pharmacy fraud scheme through trading companies that gave the appearance of legitimate business, facilitated kickbacks and bribes, and distributed profits to pharmacy owners; a Florida man received 24 months for a $33 million health care fraud and kickback scheme in Newark, NJ; a Detroit surgeon received 12 months for submitting fraudulent Medicare claims for psychotherapy services; a Missouri physician was arrested on an indictment for defrauding Medicare and Medicaid and distributing prescription drugs to friends, people with substance use disorders and sexual partners; and a Dominican national in Brockton, Mass. was charged with health care benefit fraud and aggravated identity theft. Figures and sentences span multiple defendants and distinct schemes.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, National Fraud Enforcement Division, Office of Public Affairs
cases.FraudEntity: Kaelynn Greene; Camden Newton; Betty Walker a/k/a Betty Bailey; Breanna Patterson; Jordan Greene; Valenzuela (former teacher); Corbett (former Social Security Administration employee); Leslie Victor Gentry; Suleman Yusuf Mohamed; Gandi Yusuf Mohamed; unnamed St. Louis chiropractor; unnamed Florida nursing assistant; unnamed Slidell, Louisiana man; Randon 'Romero' Williams
cases.State_County: Kentucky; Indiana; Colorado; California - San Diego; Maryland; Missouri - St. Louis; Oregon - Seaside; Arizona - Peoria; New Mexico; Alabama; Florida - Orlando; Florida - Naples; Texas - Houston; Michigan - Detroit; Michigan - West Bloomfield; Pennsylvania - Tobyhanna; Louisiana - Slidell; North Carolina - Robeson County; Minnesota - Minneapolis; South Carolina - Columbia; Massachusetts - Lynn; Iowa
cases.SchemeSummary: Weekly enforcement roundup covering multiple unrelated defendants and over $340 million in combined taxpayer fraud, including health care components: a San Diego defendant (Valenzuela) who with co-conspirators billed Medicare nearly $51 million, was paid about $20 million, paid $3.7 million in kickbacks and laundered at least $14 million; a St. Louis chiropractor sentenced to over eight years and $4.7 million restitution to Medicaid, Medicare and TRICARE for health care fraud and illegitimate prescriptions (including 94,971 oxycodone pills); a Florida nursing assistant sentenced to nine years for an $11.4 million scheme shipping unneeded orthotic braces to Medicare beneficiaries; and a Slidell, Louisiana man sentenced for billing Medicare over $6.6 million for medically unnecessary cancer genetic tests. Remaining items involve COVID-19 relief, PPP/unemployment, tax and benefit-theft frauds; figures and sentences span many defendants (longest custodial term stated: nearly 14 years in an Alabama tax fraud case).

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division and U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
cases.FraudEntity: Sanjay Kumar (Indian national, seller of counterfeit pharmaceuticals)
cases.SchemeSummary: Kumar and co-conspirators arranged sales into the United States of counterfeit Keytruda bearing counterfeit Merck marks; the product lacked the active ingredient and was ineffective. They received approximately $89,268 from undercover law enforcement agents posing as buyers, and Kumar sought to arrange further shipments before his arrest in Houston.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Indiana
cases.FraudEntity: Christine Reese (purported clinical psychologist; operator of Sanctuary Counseling)
cases.SchemeSummary: Reese used forged documents to falsely claim she was a licensed clinical psychologist with a Psy.D., obtained employment at mental health providers and later treated patients from her home under the name Sanctuary Counseling, billing Indiana Medicaid and Medicare Advantage plans for therapy she was unqualified to provide; she also stole the identities and license numbers of three legitimate practitioners to enroll in Indiana Medicaid and submit claims, resulting in $268,746.37 restitution and an 84-month sentence.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Iowa
cases.FraudEntity: Teresa Marie Johnson (licensed paramedic)
cases.SchemeSummary: A licensed paramedic diverted fentanyl from her county ambulance service employer on three occasions beginning in late 2024, tampering with vials (punctures to stoppers, adhesive on caps/crimps) so that one tested vial contained only 9.6% of its declared fentanyl, leaving patients given the diluted medication without the expected pain relief; she pleaded guilty to tampering with a consumer product, was sentenced to 30 months, fined $5,000, ordered to repay $6,000 in court-appointed attorney fees, and forfeited her Iowa paramedic license.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of Illinois
cases.FraudEntity: Sean Rondeau (chiropractor)
cases.SchemeSummary: A Jacksonville chiropractor submitted more than 2,000 separate fraudulent claims to health insurance companies, obtaining more than a quarter million dollars; he continued submitting false claims after learning he was under investigation and pressured his clients into signing false documents to conceal the scheme.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
cases.FraudEntity: Jonathan Simeon Gholston (owner/operator of marketing company)
cases.SchemeSummary: Gholston's marketing company set up tents in low-income Jacksonville areas offering free government cellphones, harvesting personal and Medicare/Medicaid insurance information from people who never requested HIV medications; the data was sent to a partnering pharmacy that generated HIV post-exposure prophylactic prescriptions signed by a nurse practitioner who never examined or spoke with the patients, then billed Medicare/Medicaid roughly $4,000 per person per month. The pharmacy paid the marketing company $200 per referral and the company paid marketers about $50 each, payable only if the claim was paid; approximately 20,316 claims caused about $24.2 million in program losses, of which Gholston received about $2,273,000 and agreed to forfeit it.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Rhode Island
cases.FraudEntity: Journey to Hope, Health and Healing (opioid treatment provider); Kenneth L. Richardson, Jr. (former CEO/owner)
cases.SchemeSummary: Outpatient opioid treatment provider billed Rhode Island Medicaid and Medicare for substance use disorder counseling and treatment services that were not provided, failing to create required treatment plans and carrying counselor caseloads so high the required counseling was physically impossible; management then altered and backdated patient records to appear compliant with accreditation and Medicaid audit requirements. Resolved by a $10.2 million FCA settlement (qui tam relators to receive ~$2.04 million).

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Idaho
cases.FraudEntity: Unidentified man using the identity of deceased child Carlos Ramon Obregon (benefit recipient)
cases.PayerName: Medicaid; Social Security Administration (SSI); USDA SNAP; U.S. Treasury (Economic Impact Payments)
cases.SchemeSummary: A man whose true identity remains unknown assumed the identity of Carlos Ramon Obregon, a child killed in 1977, obtaining a replacement Social Security card in 2000 with Obregon's SSN, date of birth and parents' names, then used that identity to enroll in and collect government benefits: roughly $177,000 in SSI (2004-2025), $91,000 in Medicaid (2005-2025), $12,000 in SNAP (2009-2025) and $3,200 in COVID-19 Economic Impact Payments, about $283,000 total. He also used Obregon's birth certificate to obtain a U.S. passport and Idaho identification cards.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, National Fraud Enforcement Division; U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: Heriberto Rodriguez (Framingham, Mass.); Mirian Chalas (U.S. citizen, Salem, N.H.); Santo Escolastico Cuello (Dominican national, Worcester, Mass.); Mario Baez Romero (Dominican national, Somerville, Mass.); Richard Odelis Vallegas Nunez (Dominican national, Allston, Mass.); Miguel Diaz Matos (Lynn, Mass.); Mitul Patel (Indian national, Worcester, Mass.); Santo Tejada Sanchez (Dominican national, Haverhill, Mass.); Jennifer Ferran (U.S. citizen, Haverhill, Mass.); Owen Landry a/k/a 'Oski' (U.S. citizen, Haverhill, Mass.); Yahaira Diaz Gomez (Dominican national, Mattapan, Mass.); five unnamed 'John Doe' defendants living under stolen identities
cases.State_County: Massachusetts - Framingham; Massachusetts - Worcester; Massachusetts - Somerville; Massachusetts - Allston (Boston); Massachusetts - Lynn; Massachusetts - Quincy; Massachusetts - Haverhill; Massachusetts - Mattapan (Boston); New Hampshire - Salem
cases.PayerName: Medicaid (MassHealth); SNAP; Social Security Administration (disability/Social Security benefits); HUD; unemployment benefits
cases.SchemeSummary: Fifteen defendants, 11 of them alleged illegal aliens, were charged with collectively obtaining more than $1.4 million in public benefits by using stolen identities, fraudulent identification/passport documents and false statements to enroll in and draw MassHealth (Medicaid), SNAP, Social Security disability, HUD housing and unemployment benefits for which they were ineligible; individual health care (MassHealth) losses ranged from about $32,717 to $266,000, and one defendant allegedly joined a staged armed robbery of a convenience store to qualify for a U Visa as a crime victim.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division, Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Louisiana (U.S. District Court, W.D. La.)
cases.FraudEntity: Priority Hospital Group LLC (Louisiana-based hospital management company); Riverside Hospital LLC and Riverside Hospital of Louisiana, Inc. (d/b/a Riverside Hospital); Post Acute Enterprises, LLC (d/b/a Mid Jefferson Extended Care Hospital); New Lifecare Hospital of North Louisiana, LLC (d/b/a Ruston Regional Specialty Hospital); an unnamed doctor (medical director/referring physician)
cases.SchemeSummary: The United States alleges in a False Claims Act complaint (originally a qui tam by a former Riverside employee) that Priority Hospital Group and three managed long term care hospitals delayed discharging Medicare patients beyond medical necessity - keeping them inpatient after treatment was complete or when a lower level of care was appropriate - because Medicare LTCH reimbursement depends in part on length of stay. It further alleges Riverside Hospital of Louisiana used medical directorship agreements and other remuneration to induce a physician's patient referrals, violating the Anti-Kickback Statute and Stark Law.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division; U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida (denaturalization complaint filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida)
cases.FraudEntity: Yoskmaikel Rodriguez Perez (operator of purported medical clinic)
cases.SchemeSummary: Rodriguez Perez operated a purported medical clinic and submitted more than $886,694 in false and fraudulent claims to Medicare, later pleading guilty to conspiracy to commit health care and wire fraud; he concealed this conduct and gave false sworn testimony during naturalization, prompting DOJ to file a four-count denaturalization complaint (one of ten denaturalization actions announced, the others involving non-health-care offenses).

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division, Office of Immigration Litigation (with U.S. Attorney's Offices for the Southern District of California, Colorado, Connecticut, Southern District of Florida, Middle District of Georgia, Northern District of Georgia, Maryland, Minnesota, Nevada, and New Jersey)
