cases.FraudEntity: Leidys Delmas Garcia (operator of physical therapy clinics) and co-conspirators
cases.SchemeSummary: Delmas Garcia admitted in criminal proceedings that she and co-conspirators established and operated 30 physical therapy clinics in Florida that billed commercial insurer Blue Cross Blue Shield approximately $36.7 million for physical therapy services that were not medically necessary and/or never provided; the present document is a civil denaturalization complaint filed against her (one of 17 unrelated denaturalization actions announced, the others involving non-health-care offenses).

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs (Criminal Division, Fraud Section)
cases.FraudEntity: AP of South Florida, LLC (APSF) (insurance brokerage); AssuredPartners, Inc. (then-parent company, civil settlement only); Paul Randall (scheme organizer/marketer); Kyrollos Mekail (pharmacist and owner of Monte Vista Pharmacy); Patricia Anderson (nurse practitioner); Candies Goode-McCoy (business owner)
cases.State_County: Florida; California - Orange County (Orange); California - Riverside County (Moreno Valley); California - Los Angeles County (West Hills); Nevada - Clark County (Las Vegas)
cases.PayerName: Federal ACA subsidy program (CMS Advanced Premium Tax Credits); Medicaid (California Medi-Cal); Florida Medicaid; IRS (COVID-19 employment tax credits)
cases.SchemeSummary: Three rolled-up actions: (1) APSF used 'street marketers' paying cash/gift cards to homeless and low-income people, then filed false ACA applications overstating income just above the poverty line and submitted false data to Florida Medicaid to manufacture denial letters triggering Special Enrollment Periods, obtaining $141.5M in unwarranted federal subsidies plus commissions/bonuses from insurers (APSF pleading guilty with $27.6M restitution; parent AssuredPartners paying $107M FCA settlement, $24.3M to the qui tam whistleblower). (2) Paul Randall, with pharmacist/owner Kyrollos Mekail and NP Patricia Anderson, exploited Medi-Cal's temporary suspension of prior authorization to bill $269,120,829 (paid ~$178.7M) through Monte Vista Pharmacy for non-contracted generic drugs in unique dosages (e.g., $13,424 for one meloxicam prescription) that were medically unnecessary and often never dispensed, paying kickbacks to patient marketers for beneficiary data and to Anderson for signing pre-filled prescriptions, then laundering proceeds; ~$126.5M in assets seized. (3) Candies Goode-McCoy filed 1,200+ tax returns claiming over $98M in fraudulent COVID-19 employee retention and paid sick/family leave credits, of which the IRS paid ~$33M; sentenced to 54 months and $26,022,188 restitution.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs / Civil Division (Enforcement and Affirmative Litigation Branch and Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section), in coordination with the Texas Attorney General
cases.FraudEntity: Texas Children's Hospital (TCH) (hospital/provider)
cases.PayerName: public and private payors (not further specified)
cases.SchemeSummary: DOJ alleged Texas Children's Hospital submitted false billings to public and private payors to obtain insurance coverage for pediatric sex-rejecting procedures (puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones), in alleged violation of the FDCA, False Claims Act and federal fraud/conspiracy statutes; TCH agreed to pay over $10 million in damages and civil penalties, stop the procedures on minors, and fund a detransition care clinic, while denying all allegations.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida; U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division, Office of Immigration Litigation
cases.FraudEntity: Mirelys Cabrera Diaz (pharmacy employee)
cases.SchemeSummary: Cabrera Diaz and co-conspirators paid kickbacks to patient recruiters who referred fraudulent prescriptions to the pharmacy where she worked, and she kept a log of amounts owed each recruiter; the pharmacy then billed Medicare Part D for prescription drugs that were never dispensed, obtaining over $6 million. She pleaded guilty in 2019, was sentenced to 29 months and over $6 million restitution, and the court revoked her 2017 naturalization on March 24, 2026 because of the pre-naturalization health care fraud conspiracy.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, National Fraud Enforcement Division; U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana; U.S. Attorney's Office, District of South Carolina
cases.FraudEntity: Spivey; Jamie McNamara (co-conspirator, genetic testing scheme); Misty Dawn Woody (employee of Vital Care medical patient transport service)
cases.SchemeSummary: Two health care fraud matters within a multi-case announcement: Spivey and co-defendant Jamie McNamara submitted $174 million in claims to Medicare for medically unnecessary cancer and cardiovascular genetic tests after luring Medicare beneficiaries into testing (Spivey sentenced, term not stated); separately, Misty Dawn Woody of Vital Care, a medical patient transport service, was indicted for copying and forging a physician's signature on over one hundred patient certification forms for patients no longer under that physician's care and submitting them to Medicare, causing over $1.8 million in false billing. Figures span two separate defendants/schemes; FraudAmt reflects the larger ($174 million) claim total.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division; U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of California; U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Colorado
cases.FraudEntity: Kaiser Foundation Health Plan Inc.; Kaiser Foundation Health Plan of Colorado; The Permanente Medical Group Inc.; Southern California Permanente Medical Group; Colorado Permanente Medical Group P.C. (Kaiser Permanente affiliates / Medicare Advantage Organizations)
cases.State_County: California - Alameda County (Oakland, headquarters); California; Colorado
cases.SchemeSummary: Kaiser allegedly mined patients' past medical histories to identify unsubmitted diagnoses and then pressured physicians to add those diagnoses to medical records via 'addenda' months or over a year after visits - diagnoses not considered or addressed at the visit - to inflate CMS risk-adjustment payments for Medicare Advantage enrollees, with physician and facility bonuses tied to diagnosis-adding goals. Settled for $556 million under the False Claims Act following qui tam suits by two former employees, whose relator share is $95 million.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Missouri
cases.FraudEntity: Ashli Forbes (owner of Forbes Realty Company LLC and Left Lane Motors LLC)
cases.SchemeSummary: Forbes submitted two PPP loan applications to Commerce Bank for her companies Forbes Realty Company LLC and Left Lane Motors LLC using fabricated payroll records, a false Schedule C, and IRS Forms 941/944 that were never filed, obtaining $206,200 and $220,400 (total $426,600); she later transferred $20,000 of the proceeds to pay an insurance bill, supporting the money laundering count, and admitted assisting in fraudulent PPP loans for four other companies totaling an additional $1,362,133.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
cases.FraudEntity: Dr. Scott Taggart Roethle (anesthesiologist)
cases.State_County: Kansas - Kansas City area; Missouri - St. Louis
cases.SchemeSummary: Overseas call centers harvested Medicare information from elderly patients; Roethle signed fraudulent orthotic brace prescriptions without examining patients while falsely claiming to be their treating physician, receiving about $30 per order (totaling $674,000 from five companies), after which suppliers shipped braces and billing companies submitted claims causing Medicare to pay at least $8 million.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Kansas
cases.FraudEntity: Tamera Ruth Powers (benefit recipient, a/k/a Minda Sue Landis)
cases.PayerName: Kansas Medicaid; Social Security Administration (Disability, SSI, Retirement Insurance Benefits); Kansas SNAP; Kansas LIEAP
cases.SchemeSummary: Powers assumed the identity of a relative who died in 1977 to obtain a Kansas ID and marry under that name, then simultaneously collected federal and state benefits under two identities, maintaining bank accounts in each name. She filed SSA disability, SSI and retirement benefit applications and Kansas Medicaid, SNAP and LIEAP applications that concealed her marriage, spousal income and prior use of another name and Social Security number, causing $137,839 in federal losses and $315,257 in Kansas losses.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Washington
cases.FraudEntity: Kelly M. Lee-Carroll (veteran benefit recipient, scheme organizer); Robert H. Nelson III (son, designated caregiver); Katoya F. Grant (sister, designated caregiver)
cases.PayerName: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA health care and disability benefit programs)
cases.SchemeSummary: Lee-Carroll falsely represented to the VA that she was bedridden, paralyzed in one leg and arm, and wheelchair-bound requiring round-the-clock care, obtaining over $11,000 per month in disability and caregiver benefits; she designated her son and sister as paid caregivers who submitted claims for caregiving hours while they were actually clocked in at other jobs or while she traveled to Las Vegas, Tennessee, Mexico and Jamaica without caregivers. Restitution figures total across all three defendants ($932,142 + $282,698 + $293,787); the longest sentence imposed was 17 months on Lee-Carroll.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of North Carolina
cases.FraudEntity: Francine Sims Super (office manager of Life Touch LLC); Life Touch LLC (substance abuse treatment company); 1st Choice Healthcare Services, LLC (drug testing lab)
cases.State_County: North Carolina - Lenoir County (Kinston); North Carolina - Wayne County (Goldsboro)
cases.SchemeSummary: Super, office manager of a substance abuse treatment company, and others paid over $1 million in gift-card kickbacks to patients based on the number of days per week they showed up for services, generating more than $12 million in Medicaid payments to Life Touch LLC; she created false documents to deceive Medicaid auditors, took kickbacks from a drug-testing lab hired for Life Touch patients, and failed to file a tax return reporting the income. Restitution totaled $15,286,912.91 to NC Medicaid plus $373,810 to the IRS.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: Laboratory Corporation of America (Labcorp) (national diagnostics testing laboratory)
cases.SchemeSummary: Labcorp marketed a 'ToxAssure Comprehensive' urine drug testing panel that ran preselected presumptive tests plus direct-to-definitive tests on the same urine sample and date of service, then billed Medicare both the all-inclusive presumptive code (CPT 80307) and the highest-tier definitive code (HCPCS G0483) each time, without first performing presumptive tests to establish medical necessity for the definitive testing.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division, Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: Laboratory Corporation of America (Labcorp) (national clinical diagnostics company)
cases.SchemeSummary: Labcorp marketed a preset urine drug testing panel, 'ToxAssure Comprehensive,' that combined presumptive testing with direct-to-definitive testing for other substances; it ran the tests simultaneously on the same urine sample and billed Medicare both the all-inclusive presumptive code (CPT 80307) and the highest-tier definitive code (HCPCS G0483) each time, performing definitive tests without a prior presumptive test to establish necessity, resulting in medically unnecessary claims. Labcorp agreed to pay $14.5 million and admitted the underlying facts.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of West Virginia
cases.FraudEntity: IntegraLabs, Inc. (Tennessee-based laboratory)
cases.SchemeSummary: Integra, an enrolled West Virginia Medicaid laboratory provider offering drug testing, allegedly submitted claims over a two-year period for medically unnecessary testing ordered by providers, specifically non-allowable specimen validity testing, resolved by a $208,624.40 False Claims Act settlement with the United States and West Virginia.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division (Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section) and U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Texas
cases.FraudEntity: Susan Hertzberg (former CEO, Boston Heart Diagnostics Corporation); Matthew Theiler (former VP of Sales, Boston Heart Diagnostics Corporation); Frederick Brown (physician); Thomas Gray Hardaway (marketer, former Boston Heart sales rep and co-owner of LGRB Management Services LLC); William Todd Hickman (marketer, former MSO owner); Ginny Jacobs (marketer, co-owner); Scott Jacobs (marketer, co-owner); S&G Staffing LLC; Jacobs Marketing Inc.
cases.State_County: Texas - Rockdale (Milam County); Texas - Frisco (Collin County); Massachusetts - Framingham (Middlesex County)
cases.SchemeSummary: Boston Heart Diagnostics' CEO and VP of Sales allegedly approved and implemented an arrangement in which marketers (including Boston Heart employees) paid doctors kickbacks disguised as managed service organization (MSO) investment distributions to induce referrals of laboratory testing, including medically unnecessary tests, routed through Texas hospitals such as Little River Healthcare and labs including True Health Diagnostics, generating claims to Medicare, Medicaid and TRICARE; Dr. Brown allegedly took payments from purported MSOs Ascend MSO of TX LLC and Indus MG LLC in exchange for test orders. Settlement figures total $2,059,055 across nine settling defendants ($600,000 each from Hertzberg and Theiler, $309,055 from Brown, $550,000 from the marketers).

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
cases.FraudEntity: Lancaster Medical LLC (former medical practice, Depew, NY)
cases.PayerName: U.S. Small Business Administration (Paycheck Protection Program)
cases.SchemeSummary: A former medical practice applied for and received a $249,290 SBA-guaranteed PPP loan in April 2020 while falsely certifying eligibility, despite having sold its assets in 2019; loan proceeds were allegedly used for impermissible purposes including personal expenses of former owners, and the loan was not repaid after forgiveness was denied. The $500,000 FCA settlement also resolves civil forfeiture litigation over a 2020 BMW X5 traceable to the loan proceeds.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of South Carolina
cases.FraudEntity: Charles McKinley Griffin; Tika Michelle Griffin (owner of Transformation Services); Kirk Nathan Evans (therapist); Transformation Services
cases.State_County: South Carolina - Lancaster County; South Carolina - Kershaw County
cases.PayerName: Medicaid (South Carolina Department of Health and Human Services)
cases.SchemeSummary: After Charles Griffin was excluded from South Carolina Medicaid, he and his wife set up Transformation Services in her name to bill Medicaid for behavioral health services; they recruited Medicaid-beneficiary children from after-school programs and camps, used therapists not authorized by the state (including Evans), and billed as if each child received hours of individual therapy when sessions were actually conducted in groups, resulting in nearly $250,000 in overlapping and nonexistent claims. Restitution of $246,335.12 (Griffins, joint and several) includes $152,669.63 joint and several with Evans.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
cases.FraudEntity: Sophia Shaklian (owner of hospice and diagnostic testing companies); Alex Alexsanian a.k.a. 'Samvel'/'Samo' (co-defendant); Chateau d'Lumina Hospice and Palliative Care; Saint Gorge Radiology; Hope Diagnostics; Direct Imaging & Diagnostics; Lab One; Labtech; Lifescan Diagnostics
cases.State_County: California - Los Angeles County (Los Angeles/Larchmont, Pasadena, Sylmar, North Hollywood, Hollywood, Burbank); California - Los Angeles County (Claremont)
cases.SchemeSummary: Shaklian and co-schemers, often using aliases, enrolled multiple sham hospice and diagnostic testing companies she owned with Medicare, used beneficiaries' information and checked their Medicare eligibility, then billed Medicare for hospice and diagnostic testing services that were medically unnecessary or never provided to beneficiaries who had never heard of the providers, causing at least $14,103,043 in losses; co-defendant Alexsanian pleaded guilty to conspiracy to launder monetary instruments and awaits sentencing.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Pennsylvania
cases.FraudEntity: John O'Brien (controlled a telecommunications company that submitted invoices); four unnamed co-defendants, including three leaders of Primary Health Network, who previously pleaded guilty
cases.SchemeSummary: O'Brien, with organization insiders, submitted fraudulent invoices - including from a telecommunications company he controlled - to Primary Health Network, a non-profit medical organization headquartered in Sharon, Pa., causing the non-profit to pay out on the bogus billings; four co-defendants, including three PHN leaders, previously pleaded guilty while O'Brien was convicted at trial on three wire fraud counts.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of New York
cases.FraudEntity: Muhammad Zishan a/k/a 'Sean'/'Shaun'/'Shawn' (operator/associate of Latham Taxi Inc.); Madiha Javed a/k/a 'Maddie'; Ghazali Shaikh; Latham Taxi Inc. (Medicaid-enrolled transportation provider)
cases.State_County: New York - Albany County; New York - Rensselaer County; New York - Warren County
cases.PayerName: Medicaid (New York State Department of Health)
cases.SchemeSummary: Operators of Latham Taxi Inc., a Medicaid-enrolled non-emergency medical transportation provider, allegedly billed New York Medicaid for 'ghost rides' and trips where recipients were never transported or never seen by a provider, and inflated reimbursement by billing group transports as multiple individual trips; they also allegedly gave recipients cash, rent abatement, and controlled substances to induce them to use Latham Taxi, yielding at least $666,281.42 in Medicaid payments.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Kentucky
cases.FraudEntity: Dashawn Dawkins (peer support specialist); Serenity Keeper's, LLC (sober home company); Delores Jordan (owner of Serenity Keepers); Jerome Davis; Lily Bell (paid the kickbacks); Ernest Williams (ran several of the sober homes)
cases.SchemeSummary: Dawkins, a peer support specialist at Serenity Keepers sober homes, took $62,750 in kickbacks for ordering urine drug tests that were billed to Kentucky Medicaid and Medicare for $2,569,946; more than 9,000 tests were ordered using the stolen provider ID and forged signature of a nurse practitioner, with no treating provider ordering or reviewing results. Serenity Keepers also billed Medicaid a flat 6 hours of peer support services per patient per day regardless of delivery and without licensed supervision, collecting $9,077,260 in behavioral health claims; five defendants total have been convicted or pleaded guilty.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
cases.FraudEntity: Natavia Boyd-Wells (owner, Touch of the Heart Home Health Care LLC); Touch of the Heart Home Health Care LLC
cases.PayerName: Missouri Medicaid Program; U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA Community Care Network)
cases.SchemeSummary: Owner of a home health company submitted hundreds of reimbursement claims to Missouri Medicaid and the VA Community Care Network for home healthcare services never provided, including on dates when veteran patients were hospitalized, and had no supporting documentation; when Medicaid auditors requested records in February 2022 she submitted fabricated documentation. Losses were at least $109,751 to Medicaid and $100,563 to the VA.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Washington
cases.FraudEntity: Dr. Eric Edward Haeger (physician, owner/operator of Central Washington Medical Associates sleep clinic); Central Washington Medical Associates
cases.State_County: Washington - Brewster (Okanogan County); Eastern District of Washington
cases.SchemeSummary: Haeger bought over 500 used, Class I recalled CPAP/BiPAP machines from online resellers, had staff and his own children pry out the recalled sound-abatement foam with screwdrivers and hooks in non-cleanroom settings, then dispensed the adulterated devices to Washington Medicaid patients through his sleep clinic; the clinic billed Medicaid for the 440 devices as if they were new and in good working order, collecting $439,272.79 of over $600,000 billed.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York
cases.FraudEntity: Roya Jafari-Hassad (licensed physician)
cases.State_County: New York - Nassau County (Great Neck); New York - Queens County (Forest Hills); New York - New York County (Manhattan)
cases.SchemeSummary: Physician charged patients hundreds of dollars in cash for monthly oxycodone prescriptions issued without legitimate medical purpose, sometimes refilling prescriptions without any appointment, and separately submitted false claims to Medicare and private insurers for medical services never rendered. Sentenced to 7 years, a $150,000 fine and $152,765 restitution.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
cases.FraudEntity: CAN USA, Inc. (company providing inspection, repair and maintenance services)
cases.State_County: Louisiana - Harvey (Jefferson Parish); New Jersey - Bergen County (Hackensack)
cases.SchemeSummary: CAN USA applied for and received a $2 million CARES Act Paycheck Protection Program loan in January 2021, falsely certifying on its application that it employed no more than 300 employees when, counting employees of its foreign affiliates, it exceeded that limit; it then obtained full forgiveness of the loan plus accrued interest. Resolved under the False Claims Act after a qui tam suit, with CAN USA paying $2,916,900 and the relator receiving $291,690.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Michigan
cases.FraudEntity: Rita Shaba; Samer Kammo (co-defendant); Christina Anasi (co-defendant)
cases.SchemeSummary: Shaba and co-conspirators submitted fraudulent Paycheck Protection Program loan applications for several business entities, misrepresenting payroll information, falsely certifying permissible use of funds, and supplying fictitious payroll, health insurance, bank and tax records; they obtained over $3 million in PPP funds, of which over $2.1 million has been recovered. Shaba received 27 months and $3,294,798.50 restitution; co-defendants Kammo and Anasi await sentencing.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
cases.FraudEntity: Protech Powder Coatings, Inc. (Delaware corporation, subsidiary of Protech Group)
cases.SchemeSummary: Protech Powder Coatings falsely certified in a second-draw Paycheck Protection Program application that it met PPP eligibility requirements when, counting affiliates' employees, it exceeded the applicable size standards; it obtained $2,016,888 in loan and loan forgiveness (including interest) and caused the government to pay $60,000 in lender processing fees. Resolved by a $2,907,643 False Claims Act settlement arising from a qui tam suit, with the relator receiving $290,764.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
cases.FraudEntity: Amanda Wilkerson (owner/operator of Divine Purpose Home Care LLC); Divine Purpose Home Care LLC
cases.SchemeSummary: The owner of a home healthcare company withheld payroll/trust fund taxes from employees' wages but failed to report and remit $57,000 to the IRS for Q3 2023 and failed to file her 2023 individual return despite over $1.6 million in income; she also submitted a PPP loan application to the SBA with a fabricated IRS Form 1040 Schedule C claiming $75,639 in 2019 gross income for a non-operational business, obtaining roughly $19,907 that was later forgiven.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland; U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maryland; DOJ Criminal Division, Fraud Section
cases.FraudEntity: Patrick Britton-Harr (owner and operator of AeroVanti and affiliated entities); AeroVanti
cases.SchemeSummary: Britton-Harr, owner of private air club AeroVanti, solicited roughly $15 million in $150,000 upfront 'Top Gun' membership payments by promising to use the funds to buy five specific aircraft, deliver aircraft titles to escrow, and provide blocks of discounted flight hours; instead he misappropriated the money for yachts, jewelry, living expenses and a $10,000/month Tampa-area rental, then concealed the scheme by obtaining a $1.5 million loan to buy an aircraft he had claimed to already own, withholding material information from the lender. (A separate May 2025 indictment charges him with health care fraud and money laundering for fraudulently billing Medicare for expensive respiratory tests; that trial is set for October 2026.)

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
cases.FraudEntity: Benjamin Jamal Washington (scheme leader); Micah Robert Lee (co-conspirator)
cases.State_County: California - Los Angeles County (Los Angeles); Maryland - Montgomery County (Bethesda); Maryland - Prince George's County (Hyattsville)
cases.FraudType: Fraudulent prescriptions via provider identity theft
FraudTypeAll: Fraudulent prescriptions via provider identity theft
cases.SchemeSummary: Washington and co-conspirators stole doctors' personal identifiers (NPI and DEA numbers, DOB, addresses), obtained fake drivers' licenses in the doctors' names and paid corrupt phone company employees for SIM swaps to capture physicians' phone numbers, then used those credentials to open fraudulent e-prescribing accounts and issue at least 5,600 bogus prescriptions for oxycodone and promethazine with codeine, which they picked up at pharmacies nationwide (including in Los Angeles) and resold for profit; Washington also stole mail and a USPS arrow key in Maryland. Co-defendant Lee pleaded guilty and awaits sentencing.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
cases.FraudEntity: Zion Oluwademilade Adeduwon; Dr. Rotimi Iluyomade (Annandale-based physician); Obioma Alozie Ndubuka; Raymono Alfonzo Russel II; Cameron Isaiah Lewis; Elhadj Malick Diallo; Kenechukwu Brian Okwara; Yared Michael Tesfaye
cases.State_County: Virginia - Fairfax County (Annandale); Virginia - Western District of Virginia; Maryland - Bowie
cases.SchemeSummary: Adeduwon and co-conspirators repeatedly visited Dr. Iluyomade's Annandale clinic and paid him roughly $300 per prescription to issue controlled-substance prescriptions (oxycodone, Tussionex, promethazine-codeine 'lean') written in fake patient names and false addresses supplied on lists, which were then transmitted to and filled at pharmacies in numerous states including at least 70 in the Western District of Virginia. Adeduwon, the first co-conspirator sentenced, received 42 months and forfeited $100,000; other charged co-conspirators await trial or sentencing.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maryland
cases.FraudEntity: Progressive Oncology & Hematology, LLC (oncology practice); Mouhamad Bazzi, MD (owner and sole provider)
cases.PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs
cases.SchemeSummary: The practice and its owner allegedly billed Medicare, Medicaid and the VA for chemotherapy drugs they never paid for (drugs supplied free by charitable organizations or grant programs for specific patients), split wastage from single-use vials across multiple patients while billing each patient as receiving their own vial, and billed for chemotherapy drugs prescribed but never administered.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: Chenguang Gong; Yalan Tang
cases.SchemeSummary: The married defendants imported misbranded performance-enhancing drugs from China using multiple post office boxes and falsified addressees to evade detection, then repackaged and sold them to U.S. customers falsely labeled 'For Research Purposes Only' while knowing customers would ingest or inject them; gross sales exceeded $2.5 million with profits over $600,000. Both were sentenced to one year and one day in prison.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: Bhamin Chhatrapati
cases.SchemeSummary: Chhatrapati and co-conspirators allegedly used telemarketers/call centers to harvest Medicare beneficiary information, generated medical documentation making it appear practitioners had legitimately prescribed medically unnecessary durable medical equipment (braces), billed Medicare over $5.1 million (of which over $2.6 million was paid), and paid the telemarketers a fee per brace order approved by Medicare.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: Ophthalmic Consultants of Boston, Inc. (ophthalmology practice)
cases.SchemeSummary: The practice billed Medicare and MassHealth for office visits in addition to intravitreal eye injections by appending Modifier 25, even when the separate evaluation-and-management service was not performed or documented, collecting extra payment beyond the injection reimbursement; resolved by a $3,902,588.28 FCA settlement arising from a qui tam suit.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Texas
cases.FraudEntity: Community Care Health Network LLC d/b/a Matrix Medical Network (in-home health assessment company); DPN USA d/b/a HealthFair (mobile health assessment company); Shahriah "James" Ekbatani (founder and manager of HealthFair)
cases.State_County: Tennessee - Nashville (Matrix headquarters); multiple states served by HealthFair mobile buses
cases.PayerName: Medicare (Medicare Advantage / Part C, via Medicare Advantage Organizations and CMS)
cases.SchemeSummary: Matrix, through in-home assessments (2014-2019), and HealthFair, through mobile-bus assessments directed by founder Ekbatani (2015-2017), reported unsupported or invalid chronic-condition diagnoses (e.g., proliferative diabetic retinopathy, drug-induced polyneuropathy, COPD, HIV/AIDS, metastatic cancer, congestive heart failure) to Medicare Advantage Organizations, which passed them to CMS for risk adjustment, inflating capitated payments. Settlement totals $56.5 million: Matrix $36.5M, HealthFair $5M, Ekbatani $15M, with whistleblowers receiving $7.3M and $3.6M.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division; U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York; U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Texas
cases.FraudEntity: Community Care Health Network LLC d/b/a Matrix Medical Network (in-home assessment provider); DPN USA d/b/a HealthFair (mobile health assessment provider); Shahriah "James" Ekbatani (founder and manager of HealthFair)
cases.SchemeSummary: Matrix conducted in-home assessments and HealthFair conducted mobile-bus assessments of Medicare Advantage beneficiaries, then reported unsupported risk-adjusting chronic-condition diagnoses (e.g., proliferative diabetic retinopathy, drug-induced polyneuropathy, atrial fibrillation, COPD; and for HealthFair HIV/AIDS, metastatic cancer, morbid obesity based only on patient attestation or contradicted by test results) to Medicare Advantage Organizations, which passed them to CMS to obtain inflated capitated risk-adjustment payments. Settlement totals $56.5M across three defendants: Matrix $36.5M, HealthFair $5M, Ekbatani $15M, resolving two qui tam actions.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of North Carolina
cases.FraudEntity: Deborah Lanell White (owner of Reginald Center of Turn Around)
cases.SchemeSummary: White, owner of Reginald Center of Turn Around, allegedly billed North Carolina Medicaid over a multi-year period for thousands of fictitious urine/drug tests that were never performed, causing a $2.8 million loss.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: Rodrigo de Medeiros Siqueira (owner of Rodrigo Beauty Inc.); Rodrigo Beauty Inc.
cases.FraudType: Unapproved drug administration by unlicensed provider
FraudTypeAll: Unapproved drug administration by unlicensed provider
cases.SchemeSummary: Med spa owner, not licensed to prescribe, dispense or administer prescription drugs, injected clients with botulinum toxin obtained from illegitimate foreign sources while falsely representing to clients that he was a licensed medical professional and misrepresenting the identity and source of the products; numerous clients developed botulism. He pleaded guilty to misbranding a drug after shipment in interstate commerce with intent to defraud or mislead; sentencing set for Aug. 12, 2026.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: Rebecca Fadanelli (owner/operator of Skin Beaute Med Spa); Skin Beaute Med Spa
cases.State_County: Massachusetts - Randolph and South Easton (Norfolk/Bristol Counties); defendant resides in Stoughton
cases.SchemeSummary: Med spa owner imported counterfeit Botox, Sculptra and Juvederm from China and Brazil and performed thousands of injections with these counterfeit drugs and devices, collecting more than $1 million in direct client payments while falsely representing to clients and employees that she was a nurse; she was in fact an unlicensed aesthetician not permitted to administer prescription drugs or devices.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Virginia
cases.FraudEntity: Chenelle Wright (owner/operator of Community Counseling Resources); Chaniece Winfield (clinical director); Community Counseling Resources (CCR)
cases.SchemeSummary: Two sisters running an after-school therapeutic day treatment program for Medicaid children directed employees to record in progress notes that services ran from 2:00pm to 7:00pm - using pre-filled note templates - although most children did not arrive until about 4:30pm, resulting in Medicaid being billed for hours of therapeutic services not provided. Wright received 41 months and Winfield 24 months in prison.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: Tactile Systems Technology, Inc. (medical device manufacturer/supplier); certain Tactile sales personnel
cases.SchemeSummary: Tactile sales personnel fabricated or amended prescribers' medical records and forged clinicians' signatures to falsely document that patients had failed conservative/basic compression therapy, making otherwise non-covered pneumatic compression devices (Entre and the more expensive Flexitouch) reimbursable by Medicare; some records were doctored to claim the basic Entre failed so the pricier Flexitouch could be billed. Resolved via a $550,959 FCA settlement from two qui tam suits, with relators receiving $129,475.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division Fraud Section / National Fraud Enforcement Division; U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Florida
cases.FraudEntity: Mark Loftis (owner of medical supply companies, chiropractor); Office of Back Pain Home Supplies (medical supply company in Drumright, Oklahoma)
cases.PayerName: Medicare; TRICARE; CHAMPVA (Civilian Health and Medical Program of the Department of Veterans Affairs)
cases.SchemeSummary: Loftis paid over $1 million to marketers using call centers to harvest personal and insurance information from elderly and disabled beneficiaries, then bought signed orders for orthotic braces and continuous glucose monitors from telemedicine doctors and nurse practitioners who never examined and often never spoke to the patients; he used those orders to bill Medicare, TRICARE and CHAMPVA over $30 million, obtaining more than $8 million, and also concealed a conspirator's management role and billed claims generated by unenrolled medical suppliers.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division and U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
cases.FraudEntity: Complete Health Partners Holdings (management services organization)
cases.SchemeSummary: Complete Health, paid a share of the risk-adjusted capitation MAOs received from CMS, disseminated incorrect coding guidance and had coders mine beneficiary medical records for additional chronic-condition diagnoses in HCC 55 (drug/alcohol dependence) and HCC 59 (major depressive, bipolar, paranoid disorders), then prompted physicians to add these unsupported diagnosis codes, inflating patient risk scores and CMS payments to the MA plans, a portion of which flowed back to Complete Health. Resolved for $14.1 million; qui tam relator Karen Bowers receives about $2,467,500.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Washington
cases.FraudEntity: Kevin Salgado (alleged leader); Haley Filler; Gabriel Tovar; Kevin Andreas; Joshua Bailey; Tyson Latchie; Kahlil Bland; Ian Newman; Edgar Adrian Hernandez; Isaac Briones; Roman Jackson; Geeneva Morandarte; Christian Ericson; Michelle Ford-Jackson
cases.State_County: Washington - Pierce County (Tacoma, Puyallup, University Place, Lakewood); Washington - Snohomish County (Lynnwood); Washington - Thurston County (Olympia); Oregon - Yamhill; California - Yucaipa
cases.SchemeSummary: Fourteen alleged members of a Tacoma-area Black Gangster Disciples-affiliated drug and gun trafficking organization were indicted after a wiretap investigation; alongside pressing and mailing counterfeit oxycodone and Xanax pills, some defendants hacked into drug distribution companies to reroute controlled-substance shipments for street sale, and one defendant allegedly paid kickbacks to an Oregon pharmacist to fill fraudulent prescriptions for oxycodone and other narcotics (defendant Isaac Briones was arrested picking up a fraudulent promethazine-with-codeine prescription in June 2025).

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Tennessee
cases.FraudEntity: Sanjeev Kumar (gynecologic oncologist, operator of Poplar Avenue Clinic)
cases.SchemeSummary: Kumar performed more than 15,000 in-office hysteroscopy-with-biopsy procedures using adulterated and misbranded devices - reusing single-use hysteroscopes and graspers and skipping required reprocessing/disinfection steps - and billed Medicare and Medicaid for the unsafe procedures, billing over $41 million and netting more than $4.8 million from the two programs between September 2019 and April 2024. Restitution hearing set for October 2, 2026.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Arizona
cases.FraudEntity: Eric Riley (owner/operator, New Horizons Behavioral Health); Britney Gooch (owner/operator, New Horizons Behavioral Health); New Horizons Behavioral Health (behavioral health clinic)
cases.PayerName: Medicaid (Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System - AHCCCS, American Indian Health Program)
cases.SchemeSummary: Through their Mesa behavioral health clinic, New Horizons Behavioral Health, Riley and Gooch billed AHCCCS's American Indian Health Program for behavioral health services never provided to AIHP patients, obtaining roughly $3.3 million; both pleaded guilty and were jointly ordered to pay $3.3 million in restitution, with Riley receiving 24 months and Gooch 12 months and one day.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Michigan
cases.FraudEntity: Mustafa Hares (surgeon); Mohammed Kazkaz
cases.State_County: Michigan - Oakland County (West Bloomfield); Michigan - Wayne County (Detroit)
cases.SchemeSummary: Hares and co-defendant Kazkaz submitted more than $7 million in Medicare claims for psychotherapy services never rendered, signing purported patient progress notes that were actually drafted by employees in Mexico rather than by medical providers. Hares received 12 months and $4.8 million restitution; Kazkaz was previously sentenced to 7 1/2 years.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Texas
cases.FraudEntity: Orlando Omar Garcia-Moya (founder/owner, Fleet Ambulance Service Inc.); Oscar Gutierrez Jr. (employee); Melody Ann Villarreal (employee); Fleet Ambulance Service Inc.
cases.State_County: Texas - Brackettville (Kinney County), Del Rio area
cases.SchemeSummary: Owner and two employees of an ambulance company billed Medicare, Medicaid and MCOs for ambulance transports by creating fraudulent run sheets for patients who were never transported, transporting patients in personal or unapproved vehicles, and listing 'ghost employees' on run sheets; billings exceeded $12.3 million (2008-2012) and $5.6 million (2013-April 2016), with $6,856,186.85 actually paid. Garcia-Moya was convicted at a bench trial on all 13 counts and sentenced to 168 months plus full restitution; co-defendants Gutierrez and Villarreal pleaded guilty and received 60 and 48 months.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan; Department of Justice, Criminal Division Fraud Section / National Fraud Enforcement Division
cases.FraudEntity: Ruby Scott (nurse, owner of Delta Home Health Care LLC); Delta Home Health Care LLC
cases.State_County: Michigan - Oakland County (Farmington Hills); Michigan - Wayne County (Detroit)
cases.SchemeSummary: Scott bribed a Detroit hospital discharge nurse (over $130,000 total, about $300 per successfully billed patient, paid via CashApp, PayPal, check and cash) to fax confidential Medicare patient records to her home health agency; she then billed Medicare for home health services using the stolen patient profiles, falsely representing that physicians had certified the patients as homebound and eligible when no doctor had evaluated them, and in some cases billing for patients who never received services, causing about $1.6 million in losses (Medicare paid over $1.2 million on claims for patients with no maintained files).

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Illinois
cases.FraudEntity: Unnamed defendant (charged in Medicare COVID-19 test kit scheme); unnamed health care provider (Illinois Medicaid behavioral health scheme); Burhan Mirza; Kashif Iqbal; Seung Han Lim (chiropractor) and his clinic
cases.State_County: Illinois - Chicago area (Northern District of Illinois)
cases.PayerName: Medicare; Illinois Medicaid; Blue Cross Blue Shield of Illinois; private health care benefit programs
cases.SchemeSummary: Mid-year report summarizing several Northern District of Illinois health care fraud matters: one defendant charged with billing Medicare roughly $240 million in under six months for over-the-counter COVID-19 test kits never provided or never requested by beneficiaries; a provider charged with billing Illinois Medicaid more than $75 million for behavioral health counseling and therapy never rendered; Burhan Mirza and Kashif Iqbal charged with using nominee-owned laboratories and durable medical equipment companies to submit about $10 million in claims to Medicare and private insurers for items and services not provided; and chiropractor Seung Han Lim convicted of billing Blue Cross Blue Shield of Illinois over $600,000 for services not rendered. Figures span multiple defendants; the office also states approximately $2.135 billion in charged health care fraud losses district-wide since April 2025.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
cases.FraudEntity: Habroon Habib (registrant/operator of Around The World Solutions LLC); Around The World Solutions LLC
cases.PayerName: Medicare Advantage (Medicare Part C) plans operated by private insurers
cases.SchemeSummary: Habib registered a Connecticut shell company and opened a bank account, and an individual in Pakistan submitted approximately $1.9 million in claims to Medicare Advantage plans for durable medical equipment (orthotics and braces) that roughly 413 beneficiaries in 36 states never requested, consented to, or received; about $680,571 was paid into the company account, and Habib wired $425,000 of it to Pakistan through an unlicensed money transmitting business.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Wisconsin
cases.FraudEntity: Antonio Franklin (benefit recipient)
cases.PayerName: Social Security Administration (Title XVI disability benefits); Wisconsin Department of Health Services (Wisconsin Supplemental Security Income and IRIS program)
cases.SchemeSummary: Franklin concealed from the government an undisclosed bank account through which more than $1 million flowed between January 2020 and March 2025, failing to report income/assets that would have made him ineligible, and thereby collected nearly $300,000 in SSA Title XVI disability, Wisconsin SSI, and IRIS self-directed personal care benefits; the court ordered restitution equal to the benefits unlawfully received.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Wisconsin
cases.FraudEntity: Lenard R. Monroe (owner, Wellness Personal Care Service); Wellness Personal Care Service (home healthcare agency); Phillip Daniels (codefendant, patient referrer)
cases.PayerName: Wisconsin Medicaid; U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA COVID relief)
cases.SchemeSummary: Over at least three years, Monroe's home healthcare company Wellness Personal Care Service billed Wisconsin Medicaid for thousands of hours of in-home personal care services that were never provided, and Monroe paid codefendant Phillip Daniels over $600,000 in kickbacks to refer clients to the agency; he also used his Medicaid provider status to obtain roughly $247,000 in HRSA COVID relief funds intended for pandemic-harmed providers and spent proceeds on luxury purchases including a Dodge Demon drag car. Restitution of $2,543,216.62 to Wisconsin Medicaid and $247,167.90 to HRSA was ordered against Monroe.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, National Fraud Enforcement Division (Fraud Division, Health Care Fraud Section) and U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Minnesota
cases.FraudEntity: 15 unnamed defendants, including owners of child care centers and various Minnesota Medicaid providers (2 charged in the EIDBI autism scheme; 1 in the Integrated Community Supports scheme; 2 in the Individualized Home Supports scheme; 8 in the Housing Stabilization Services scheme, some traveling from Pennsylvania; 2 in child care subsidy schemes)
cases.PayerName: Medicaid (Minnesota Medical Assistance / Minnesota Health Care Programs, including EIDBI, Integrated Community Supports, Individualized Home Supports and Housing Stabilization Services); Minnesota Great Start Compensation Support Payment Program; federal Child Care Assistance Program
cases.SchemeSummary: Coordinated takedown of 15 defendants across five Minnesota Medicaid and child care programs totaling over $90 million in intended loss: an approximately $46.6 million EIDBI autism scheme in which defendants paid kickbacks to parents, diagnosed children with autism regardless of medical necessity and billed for autism services never provided; a $1.4 million Integrated Community Supports scheme billing for 24-hour care not rendered (including a recipient found deceased a day after being billed); an over $22 million Individualized Home Supports scheme in which defendants bought 20+ residences, concealed their prohibited ownership interest from Medicaid, housed beneficiaries to harvest their information, and billed for services not provided as represented, spending proceeds on real estate, luxury cars and jewelry; approximately $15.7 million in Housing Stabilization Services billing fraud; and $425,000 (Great Start program) plus $4.6 million (Child Care Assistance Program) child care subsidy frauds.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Alabama
cases.FraudEntity: Robert L. Crites (owner of Health Services Plus and TriCom, LLC; contractor of Extraordinary Scripts, Inc.)
cases.State_County: Mississippi - Batesville (Panola County); Alabama - Montgomery County (Montgomery)
cases.SchemeSummary: Crites and associates of Extraordinary Scripts recruited TRICARE beneficiaries nationwide and referred them to Cloverland Pharmacy in Montgomery, Alabama, which paid per-referral commissions/kickbacks; TRICARE sustained $5,447,474.94 in losses, and the court entered a $31,039,134.82 judgment (treble damages plus civil penalties) against Crites, the last remaining defendant after five co-defendants settled.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division and U.S. Attorney's Office for the Central District of California
cases.FraudEntity: Modern Nuclear Inc. (mobile PET scan provider)
cases.SchemeSummary: MNI allegedly paid referring cardiologists above-fair-market-value supervision fees for mobile PET scans - including paying them for time spent treating other patients, time off-site, and for services rarely or never provided - to induce referrals, then billed federal health care programs for the resulting scans; resolved via an $8,334,350.71 ability-to-pay settlement (plus future revenue-based amounts) and a five-year Corporate Integrity Agreement following a qui tam suit.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of California
cases.FraudEntity: Blanca Estela Cardenas (nurse practitioner, owner of Mobile Care Medical Providers, LLC and B&R Wound Care, Inc.); Raquel Pasillas (daughter, operational leadership at the businesses); Mobile Care Medical Providers, LLC; B&R Wound Care, Inc.
cases.State_County: California - San Diego County (San Diego/Chula Vista)
cases.SchemeSummary: Indictment alleges the businesses billed Medicare roughly $9.5 million (receiving about $5.5 million) for mobile wound care services and costly skin substitute allografts under nurse practitioner Cardenas' NPI, falsely representing her as the rendering provider while she was incarcerated in federal prison; her unlicensed daughter allegedly performed the services. More than $4.7 million of proceeds were allegedly diverted through cash withdrawals, personal bank deposits, and rent payments.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Texas
cases.FraudEntity: Judy Terecia Sanchez (mother/guardian of Medicaid beneficiary)
cases.PayerName: Texas Medicaid (Texas Health and Human Services)
cases.SchemeSummary: After the certified nurse aide she hired for her quadriplegic son resigned within two weeks, Sanchez falsified time sheets for six years as if the aide were still providing home health attendant care, submitted them to Texas Medicaid, had the checks payable to the aide mailed to a post office box she controlled, and then forged and cashed them, obtaining $227,377 while her son received no care.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Tennessee; United States District Court for the Eastern District of Tennessee at Knoxville
cases.FraudEntity: Barbara A. Smith (clinic office manager); Jared Grant Riddle (licensed pharmacist); Brian M. Woods (marketer); George Ernest Riddle (owner of United Apothecary, LLC); United Apothecary, LLC d/b/a Riddle Drugs / Riddle Express Pharmacy
cases.State_County: Tennessee - Knox County (Knoxville); Tennessee - Anderson County (Clinton, Oliver Springs); Tennessee - Jefferson County (Dandridge)
cases.PayerName: Medicare Part D; other drug plans and pharmacy benefit managers
cases.SchemeSummary: A pharmacist created a drug formulary of high-reimbursement products (pain creams and chlorzoxazone 250 mg), paid a marketer off-the-books cash bonuses per signed formulary, and the marketer paid a pain clinic's office manager cash to alter signed formularies (adding unprescribed drugs and refills) and to create wholly forged formularies with handwritten or photocopied provider signatures; the pharmacy billed these prescriptions to drug plans and PBMs, collecting about $7.37 million including roughly $4.8 million from Medicare Part D. In a related case, the pharmacy owner and his son paid kickbacks to out-of-state marketers for signed prescriptions billed to Medicare Part D for about $1.32 million. Restitution figures total across four defendants; longest sentence was 37 months (Smith), with 33 months each for Riddle and Woods and 15 months for Ernest Riddle.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Washington
cases.FraudEntity: MultiCare Health System (hospital and healthcare system operating MultiCare Deaconess Hospital and MultiCare Rockwood Clinic); Dr. Jason A. Dreyer (neurosurgeon)
cases.State_County: Washington - Spokane County (Spokane); Washington - Pierce County (Tacoma)
cases.PayerName: Medicare; Washington Medicaid; TRICARE (Department of Defense); Federal Employees Health Benefits Program (FEHBP); Department of Veterans Affairs
cases.SchemeSummary: MultiCare allowed neurosurgeon Dr. Jason Dreyer to perform a high volume of medically unnecessary complex spinal surgeries at Deaconess Hospital between 2019 and 2021 - ignoring physician-assistant patient safety complaints and explicit federal investigator warnings about falsified diagnoses - and billed Medicare, Medicaid and other federal health programs for those surgeries, while paying Dreyer compensation tied to the number and complexity of surgeries performed. MultiCare will pay $3.728 million (including $1.6 million restitution), with the qui tam relator receiving $633,760; related prior settlements were $22.7 million with Providence Health & Services and more than $1.1 million with Dr. Dreyer.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, National Fraud Enforcement Division, Health Care Fraud Unit (trials in the Southern District of Florida, Central District of California, Eastern District of Michigan, Eastern District of New York, and Middle District of Tennessee)
cases.FraudEntity: Brett Blackman (founder and CEO of HealthSplash/DMERx telehealth platform); Gary Cox (co-defendant, convicted at prior trial); Dr. Violetta Mailyan (physician); Ruby Scott (licensed nurse, owner of Delta Home Health Care LLC); Tony Brown-Arkah (owner of American Medical Centers); Olga Popovych (manager of Brooklyn physical therapy clinics); Heather Marks (advanced registered nurse practitioner, Lifeforce Pain and Wellness)
cases.State_County: Florida; California; Michigan; New York - Kings County (Brooklyn); Tennessee - Carthage
cases.SchemeSummary: Six separate jury trial convictions rolled into one announcement totaling over $1.1 billion in losses: Blackman's DMERx platform used foreign call centers and spam mailers to push medically unnecessary orthotic braces on Medicare beneficiaries and paid telemedicine companies kickbacks for doctor-signed orders falsely certifying exams (over $1 billion billed, $450 million paid); Mailyan billed Medicare over $45 million for Botox injections never given, including while on vacation, for an incarcerated patient and on days her clinic was closed, then fabricated back-dated consent forms for a grand jury subpoena (forfeiture of vehicles, $7.3 million in brokerage accounts and four properties); Scott paid a hospital discharge nurse over $130,000 via CashApp/PayPal/check/cash for stolen Medicare patient records and billed home health with fabricated physician homebound certifications ($1.6 million loss); Brown-Arkah's Brooklyn substance abuse clinic billed Medicare and Medicaid $52 million for visits by a non-clinician and never-provided services while diverting Suboxone and taking lab referral kickbacks; Popovych paid ambulette drivers cash for Medicare patient referrals and falsified records showing therapists treated patients on days they were absent (over $8 million paid 2018-2020); Marks prescribed nearly one million opioid pills at a rural Tennessee pain clinic. Figures span multiple defendants; the longest custodial sentence noted is 15 years for co-defendant Gary Cox.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Michigan
cases.FraudEntity: Hasan "Lucas" Seyhun (Chief Operating Officer, Fast Lab Technologies); Cemhan "Jimmy" Biricik (CEO, Fast Lab Technologies, previously charged); Dr. Martin Perlin (Medical Director, previously charged); Emad Hamdan (supervisor, Medex Pharmacy); Raeyfah Baiz (pharmacist-in-charge, Medex Pharmacy); Rabih Hamdan (owner, Medex Pharmacy); Christopher Dzialo; Reno Dandy a/k/a "RJ" (operator, Grace Medical Clinic PLLC); Francina Kirk a/k/a "Keisha" (operator, Grace Medical Clinic PLLC); Dr. Chinoy (prescriber at Grace); McLaren Health Care Corporation and related entities; Jason Herzog (former CEO, Avertest, LLC d/b/a Averhealth)
cases.State_County: Michigan - Wayne County (Detroit, Dearborn Heights, Grosse Pointe Farms, Eastpointe); Michigan - Wayne County (Canton area); Michigan - Oakland County (Pontiac); Southeast Michigan; Florida - Miami-Dade County (Miami); Nevada - Washoe County (Reno); Virginia - Henrico County (Glen Allen)
cases.PayerName: Medicare; Michigan Medicaid (Michigan Department of Health and Human Services); Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan; private health insurer
cases.SchemeSummary: Part of the 2026 national takedown (455 defendants, over $6.5 billion in intended loss), the Eastern District of Michigan announced six matters: Fast Lab Technologies executives allegedly billed insurers $566 million for COVID-19 laboratory testing never rendered or not as represented and laundered the proceeds; Medex Pharmacy supervisors and its pharmacist-in-charge allegedly billed Medicare, Medicaid and BCBS of Michigan about $1.9 million for prescriptions not medically necessary or never dispensed (pharmacy lacked inventory); Christopher Dzialo allegedly submitted eight fraudulent Direct Member Reimbursement claims worth $158,514 to his own insurer for drugs and procedures he never received; Grace Medical Clinic operators allegedly paid a physician who e-prescribed over 400,000 opioid dosage units to "patients" he never saw. Civil settlements: McLaren Health Care $1.9 million for failing to timely repay overpayments and former Averhealth CEO Jason Herzog $150,000 for false claims to Michigan DHHS over improper positive oral fluid drug test results.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Florida
cases.FraudEntity: Edward Scott Morrison (licensed physician)
cases.SchemeSummary: Indicted on 41 counts of distributing and dispensing controlled substances: as a licensed physician, Morrison allegedly wrote and signed prescriptions for at least 25,500 controlled substance pills (over 22,000 opioid and over 3,000 stimulant pills, including oxycodone, hydrocodone, amphetamine, alprazolam and testosterone) on request from patients or third parties, without physical examinations, without reviewing prescribing records, and without creating any records of the encounters.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida (with DOJ Health Care Fraud Unit Florida Strike Force)
cases.FraudEntity: Casilda Muniz Rodriguez (clinic set-up facilitator); Dr. Jason Finkelstein (cardiologist, medical director of cardiovascular testing company; owner of Cardiovascular Testing Services PA and Cardiovascular Healthcare Associates PA); Eduardo Javier Ibarra Arrowsmith (posed as licensed physician); Ibrahim Hilmi (operator of ABRH Care, Inc. and Sunshine Senior Solutions LLC); Giorgi Kimeridze (money launderer); Laura Seiler-Anstett (biller/consultant); Rajiv Shah (owner of ACC-Q Data, LLC billing company); Anthony Tursi (call center owner); Yilian Cruz (co-owner, De La Cruz Mental Health LLC); Inti Cruz (co-owner, De La Cruz Mental Health LLC); Adaimis Perez Arencibia (therapist); Rene Yartu Couceiro (therapist)
cases.State_County: Florida - Miami-Dade County (Miami, Hialeah, Miami Lakes); Florida - Broward County (Coral Springs); Florida - Palm Beach County (Palm Beach Gardens, Boynton Beach); Texas - Tarrant County (Fort Worth)
cases.PayerName: Medicare; Medicare Advantage Organizations; Medicare Supplemental Insurers; Florida Medicaid; Federal Employees Health Benefits Program (FEHBP); private insurers
cases.SchemeSummary: As part of DOJ's 2026 National Health Care Fraud Takedown (455 defendants nationwide, over $6.5 billion in claims), 12 defendants were charged in the Southern District of Florida in schemes totaling over $4 billion: sham clinics enrolled with Medicare under nominee owners billed over $117 million for skin substitutes/amniotic wound allografts never provided (Medicare paid over $55 million); 'bust-out' DME companies (ABRH Care and Sunshine Senior Solutions) billed at least $3.76 billion for equipment and wound dressings never supplied with proceeds wired to Hong Kong; a cardiologist billed roughly $89 million for cardiovascular screenings of student athletes with fabricated diagnoses and rubber-stamped test reviews; billers submitted $58.3 million and over $64 million in medically unnecessary orthotic brace/DME claims procured by kickbacks; a call center sold telemarketed doctors' orders for $62 million in genetic tests; and Miami mental health clinics paid cash 'donations' to elderly Medicaid/Medicare beneficiaries and falsified attendance sheets for PSR and TMS sessions not provided. Figures span multiple defendants; $27,425,929 was seized from 12 South Florida clinics.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs (National Fraud Enforcement Division / Health Care Fraud Unit), with 56 U.S. Attorneys' Offices and 45 State Attorneys General's Offices/Medicaid Fraud Control Units
cases.FraudEntity: 455 defendants charged nationwide, including 90 doctors and other licensed medical professionals; named defendants include Ibrahim Hilmi (transnational catheter/DME scheme, apprehended in Kyrenia); Herb Kimble (fugitive, telemedicine/DME scheme); Khalid Satary (genetic testing scheme, fugitive); Emylee Thai (genetic testing scheme, fugitive); an unnamed Vice President of Sales of an allograft company (D. Ariz.); an unnamed nurse practitioner (S.D. Tex.); three defendants in a Middle District of Florida allograft scheme; an unnamed hospice owner and two marketers (C.D. Cal.); a medical director of a cardiovascular testing practice (S.D. Fla.); eight defendants in a New York social adult day care scheme (E.D.N.Y.); a co-owner of a mental health company (E.D. Va.); a behavioral health biller (Illinois Medicaid); a personal care attendant (Alaska)
cases.State_County: Arizona; Texas (Southern District); Florida (Middle and Southern Districts); Illinois; California (Central District); New York - Kings County (Brooklyn); Virginia (Eastern District); Alaska; Pennsylvania (Eastern District); South Carolina; cases in 56 federal districts and 45 U.S. states and territories
cases.PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid (including New York Medicaid, Illinois Medicaid, Virginia Medicaid, Alaska Medicaid); private insurers
cases.SchemeSummary: Nationwide takedown aggregating 455 defendants and over $6.5 billion in alleged false claims: billing Medicare billions for medically unnecessary amniotic wound allografts driven by ~40% kickbacks to marketers and providers (including applying grafts to hospice patients and areas larger than the wound), a $906 million single-nurse-practitioner allograft scheme, $3.7 billion in claims for urinary catheters and DME never provided, a $27.7 million hospice scheme using purchased decedent data and back-dated records to bill for the recently deceased, $67 million in Illinois Medicaid behavioral health claims for 500+ counseling hours per day never rendered, $38 million in New York Medicaid social adult day care claims for beneficiaries never served, $49 million in Virginia Medicaid crisis-stabilization billing procured by bribing homeless people with hotel stays, and $89 million in falsified cardiovascular testing of student athletes. Figures span hundreds of defendants; settlement figure combines 48 civil monetary payment settlements over $73 million and civil settlements with 31 defendants totaling $23 million, with over $182 million in assets seized.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
cases.FraudEntity: Holly Broussard (sales representative for a Louisiana-based diagnostic laboratory); Dr. Christopher Whipple (licensed physician); Jaquala Robertson (employer under Medicaid Self Direction Program); Kirstan Wells (personal care service worker); Asha Clark (direct service worker, Medicaid Self Direction Program)
cases.State_County: Louisiana - Shreveport; Louisiana - New Orleans; Louisiana - Hammond; Louisiana - Mount Hermon
cases.SchemeSummary: Five defendants charged in the Eastern District of Louisiana portion of the 2026 national takedown: Broussard, a lab sales rep, solicited orders for medically unnecessary respiratory pathogen panel tests bundled with COVID-19 tests from rural providers, nursing homes and assisted living facilities that needed only COVID testing, causing over $51.7 million in claims of which the lab was paid over $28.4 million; Dr. Whipple billed Medicare at least $5.9 million for in-person care he did not provide (including while out of state and after a patient had died) and used other providers' identities without permission; and three state defendants (Robertson, Wells, Clark) submitted or approved false Medicaid Self Direction personal care service claims for times when recipients were in day care or incarcerated, totaling about $12,144 paid.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice - Civil Division and Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
cases.FraudEntity: AP of South Florida, LLC (APSF) (insurance brokerage); AssuredPartners, Inc. (then-parent company); Cory Lloyd (former president of APSF)
cases.PayerName: Federal government - Affordable Care Act Advanced Premium Tax Credit subsidies (CMS); Florida Medicaid
cases.SchemeSummary: APSF used 'street marketers' who recruited homeless, unemployed and addicted individuals at shelters, bus stops and drug treatment clinics - sometimes paying cash or gift cards - and then submitted ACA marketplace applications falsely inflating consumers' income to just above the federal poverty line so the plans would be fully subsidized, generating $141.5 million in improper Advanced Premium Tax Credits and commissions/bonuses from insurers; APSF also filed false Florida Medicaid applications designed to be denied so the denial letters could trigger Special Enrollment Periods, and submitted false responses to CMS income verification inquiries. Figures span the corporate resolutions: APSF agreed to plead guilty to major fraud and pay $27.6 million restitution while parent AssuredPartners paid $107 million to settle FCA allegations (whistleblower share $24.3 million); former president Cory Lloyd was convicted at trial in November 2025 and sentenced to 20 years.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Oklahoma
cases.FraudEntity: Jeremy Michael Bowles (operator of 3 pharmacies); Dameion Ray (grant applicant/property owner); Tamara Reid (property owner); Quincy Reid (property owner)
cases.PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; Child Care Development Block Grant Program (Oklahoma Department of Human Services)
cases.SchemeSummary: Two matters announced together: Jeremy Bowles was indicted on 16 counts of health care fraud for submitting false reimbursement claims for COVID-19 tests to Medicare and Medicaid through three pharmacies he controlled; separately, a civil forfeiture complaint targets Tulsa real property allegedly bought with about $300,000 of a $600,000 Child Care Desert Grant (Child Care Development Block Grant funds) awarded to Dameion Ray in December 2022.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Nevada
cases.FraudEntity: David Ralph Webber (owner/operator of Passion Plus Enterprises Inc. and Whole Science Health); Passion Plus Enterprises Inc.; Whole Science Health
cases.SchemeSummary: Webber allegedly used two companies he owned to import hundreds of thousands of misbranded prescription capsules/tablets containing sildenafil and tadalafil made at unregistered facilities in India, falsely declaring wire transfers to manufacturers as payments for 'business management consultancy services' and paying a packaging company to label the products '100% Natural' with false ingredients and no prescription requirement; he then sold them to smoke shops, convenience stores, and adult novelty stores across the southwestern U.S. and directly via his website, generating over $1.9 million in revenue.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Georgia; U.S. Department of Justice, Antitrust Division (Washington Criminal Section)
cases.FraudEntity: Scott G. Srodes (former employee of a shelving and storage distributor); unnamed co-conspirators
cases.State_County: Georgia - Valdosta (Moody Air Force Base); Nevada - Las Vegas (Nellis Air Force Base)
cases.PayerName: U.S. Air Force / U.S. Department of War (Defense Logistics Agency Facilities Maintenance, Repair, and Operations Program)
cases.SchemeSummary: Srodes and co-conspirators exchanged pricing information and submitted collusive, non-competitive bids—at times telling each other exactly what price to quote—for the sale of shelving and storage products for healthcare facilities at Moody AFB and aircraft maintenance facilities at Nellis AFB, projects worth over $1.8 million funded through the Defense Logistics Agency's Facilities Maintenance, Repair, and Operations Program.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
cases.FraudEntity: 14 unnamed indicted individuals, including a home health aide accused of stealing a client's Social Security retirement and Veterans Administration benefits and the owner of a pest control business accused of fraudulently receiving disability benefits
cases.State_County: Missouri - Eastern District of Missouri (St. Louis)
cases.PayerName: Social Security Administration; U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs
cases.SchemeSummary: Fourteen defendants were indicted for collectively defrauding the government of about $1 million through disability fraud, pandemic-relief fraud and theft of Social Security and other benefits, including a home health aide who allegedly stole a client's Social Security retirement and VA benefits, a pest control business owner who allegedly obtained disability benefits fraudulently, and others who continued collecting benefits paid to deceased beneficiaries.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
cases.FraudEntity: Nicholas Ortega Munoz; Isabella Valderrama Ospina; BLK Graphics Group (sham company); Technology SD (sham company)
cases.SchemeSummary: Two defendants used two sham companies, BLK Graphics Group and Technology SD, with rotating bank accounts at multiple institutions to receive deposits from pornographic websites (including 'token' payouts for adult performers) and rapidly transfer over $62 million to shell companies in Colombia, without registering as money transmitting businesses with FinCEN. Both defendants pleaded guilty; sentencing pending.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
cases.FraudEntity: Ritesh Kalra (internist / physician)
cases.State_County: New Jersey - Bergen County (Fair Lawn); New Jersey - Hudson County (Secaucus)
cases.SchemeSummary: Physician allegedly ran a pill mill, issuing more than 31,000 oxycodone prescriptions (including to an incarcerated patient with no contact and in exchange for sexual favors), and billed New Jersey Medicaid for in-person office visits that never occurred, supported by false electronic progress notes with fabricated dates of service and identical exam notes lacking vital signs.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of New York
cases.FraudEntity: Bryan Otero (conspirator); Cierra Washington (co-defendant, pleaded guilty); Raven White (co-defendant, pleaded guilty)
cases.State_County: New York; New Jersey - Wood Ridge (defendant's residence); pharmacies throughout the Northeastern United States
cases.SchemeSummary: Otero and co-conspirators stole personally identifiable information of Medicaid beneficiaries and used it to fraudulently obtain prescription medications from pharmacies across the Northeastern U.S., with the drug claims billed to New York Medicaid, causing nearly $4 million in Medicaid losses and tens of thousands of dollars in pharmacy losses. Otero was sentenced to 48 months; over $1.1 million in assets were recovered from him and he was ordered to pay an additional $3 million restitution; co-defendants Washington and White pleaded guilty and await sentencing.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
cases.FraudEntity: Nestor E. Jaime (pharmacy owner)
cases.SchemeSummary: Through a Paterson, NJ pharmacy he owned, Jaime submitted hundreds of false Medicare claims for Dificid (over $4,000 per prescription) that the pharmacy never purchased or dispensed, on behalf of beneficiaries who were never prescribed it, falsely inserting providers' unique provider numbers to make the prescriptions appear legitimate; Medicare paid about $2.5 million, spent on luxury vehicles and personal expenses.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
cases.FraudEntity: Taejin Kim (licensed physical therapist)
cases.SchemeSummary: Kim, a licensed physical therapist, let her license and business bank accounts be used to submit false claims to Amtrak's employee health plan for physical therapy services never provided and medically unnecessary, in exchange for a share of proceeds; co-conspirators paid cash kickbacks to Amtrak employees for use of their insurance information. The plan paid about $2,253,453 on claims tied to Kim and over $11 million overall across the 19 prosecuted participants; Kim received 12 months plus one day and restitution over $2.2 million.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs; National Fraud Enforcement Division; USAO - New Mexico
cases.FraudEntity: Dorothea Irving (driver for non-emergency medical transportation company)
cases.SchemeSummary: Irving, a driver for a non-emergency medical transport company, submitted false trip records to New Mexico Medicaid claiming she and her children were beneficiaries lacking transportation, billing for trips that never occurred and for acting as an attendant on her children's trips; drivers signed forms falsely stating they drove each other, often to distant Alcoholics Anonymous meetings, and the company billed each passenger as a separate trip. The company billed approximately $3,957,788 and received about $4,142,942, of which Irving received roughly $980,901.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Arizona
cases.FraudEntity: Thvoughn Lynden Curry (co-owner, 1 Family Clinic, LLC); Alexis Daneen Curry (purported 100% owner and managing employee, 1 Family Clinic, LLC); 1 Family Clinic, LLC (outpatient behavioral health clinic)
cases.PayerName: Medicaid (Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System - AHCCCS)
cases.SchemeSummary: The Currys enrolled their purported Mesa outpatient behavioral health clinic, 1 Family Clinic LLC, as an AHCCCS provider using a false application that hid Thvoughn Curry's ownership and his outstanding felony fraud warrant, then billed AHCCCS in a uniform pattern for behavioral health services never provided - averaging over 12 hours of service per member per day at a clinic open only eight hours on weekdays - collecting more than $12 million that they spent on properties and luxury vehicles including a $300,000+ Lamborghini Urus; both defendants were convicted of conspiracy, health care fraud and money laundering, with sentencing set for May 4, 2026.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Arizona
cases.FraudEntity: Thvoughn Lynden Curry (owner/managing employee of 1 Family Clinic, LLC); Alexis Daneen Curry (purported sole owner and manager); 1 Family Clinic, LLC (outpatient behavioral health clinic)
cases.State_County: Arizona - Maricopa County (Mesa; defendants of New River)
cases.PayerName: Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System (AHCCCS) - Arizona Medicaid, American Indian Health Plan
cases.SchemeSummary: The Currys enrolled 1 Family Clinic as an AHCCCS provider using a false application concealing Thvoughn Curry's ownership/managing role (he had an outstanding state felony fraud warrant), then billed AHCCCS's American Indian Health Plan in a uniform, nearly identical pattern averaging more than 12 hours of service per member per day for licensed substance abuse therapy that was never provided, collecting over $12 million that was spent on properties and luxury vehicles including a $300,000+ Lamborghini Urus. Both defendants were convicted at a bench trial; Thvoughn received 88 months and Alexis 70 months, with joint restitution of over $12 million.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division Fraud Section / National Fraud Enforcement Division
cases.FraudEntity: Elnar Zarbailov (business owner, fixer and money launderer for a transnational criminal organization); foreign-based Transnational Criminal Organization (Russia-based)
cases.SchemeSummary: A Russia-based organization used nominee owners equipped with false sale and corporate registration documents to open U.S. bank accounts for fraudulent durable medical equipment companies, then deposited Medicare and private insurer reimbursement checks from the DME fraud and moved them to shell companies and overseas banks; Zarbailov deposited and transferred nearly $1.5 million in proceeds from five DME companies, including to foreign accounts, and was sentenced to 37 months and $1,457,898 forfeiture.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of New York
cases.FraudEntity: Ezriel Green (finance manager for an assisted living facility)
cases.State_County: New York - Mohawk (assisted living facility); defendant of Brooklyn, New York
cases.PayerName: New York Medicaid; U.S. Treasury Department
cases.SchemeSummary: While employed to manage the finances of an assisted living facility in Mohawk, NY, Green allegedly obtained and cashed over $573,000 in checks payable to the facility issued by the U.S. Treasury and New York Medicaid, converting funds intended for facility operations and elderly resident care to his own use.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of New York
cases.FraudEntity: Ciera Washington; Raven White; Bryan Otero
