cases.SchemeSummary: After a car accident, Williams spent six years lying to the elderly victim and the victim's friend about fabricated injuries, surgeries, medical equipment (walker, in-home elevator) and medical bills allegedly caused by the crash, and impersonated insurance agents via disguised-number text messages promising reimbursement, inducing the victim to pay more than $500,000 (total intended loss $672,086) which Williams spent on restaurants, travel and gambling.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia
cases.FraudEntity: Michelle Shropshire (WMATA train operator, scheme organizer); Harlisha Jones (codefendant, WMATA employee); six other WMATA employees
cases.SchemeSummary: Over about four years, a WMATA train operator prepared and submitted fraudulent disability and health care claims to AFLAC for herself and numerous WMATA coworkers for injuries never suffered, fabricating medical records and forging real doctors' signatures while the claimants kept working and drawing WMATA paychecks; each co-conspirator paid her roughly 20 percent of the fraudulent payout. Figures cover the lead defendant, who caused at least $362,035.14 in losses and personally profited $80,520.36; a codefendant and six other employees also pleaded guilty.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia
cases.FraudEntity: Michelle Shropshire (WMATA train operator, scheme organizer); Harlisha Jones (WMATA train operator); five other former WMATA employees (previously pleaded guilty)
cases.PayerName: American Family Life Assurance Company of Columbus (AFLAC)
cases.SchemeSummary: Two WMATA train operators used Jones's AFLAC health and short-term disability policies to submit claims for injuries, treatments and disability periods that never occurred, supporting them with forged medical excuse notes and physician's statements bearing real doctors' names and forged signatures; AFLAC paid Jones about $58,750 and she kicked back roughly 20% to Shropshire, who ran the same scheme with five other WMATA employees for at least $362,035 in total payouts. Shropshire was later sentenced to 24 months in prison per an associated release.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of California
cases.FraudEntity: Julianna C. Lung (marketer/seller of hearing devices)
cases.PayerName: Federal Employees Health Benefits (FEHB) program health plans
cases.SchemeSummary: Lung sold hearing protection devices to Border Patrol agents, other federal employees and their families, telling buyers the devices were for hearing protection rather than treatment, then submitted approximately 385 claims to FEHB plans falsely representing that the beneficiaries had hearing loss or tinnitus requiring medically necessary hearing aids; plans paid about $2,500 per device, totaling roughly $962,500.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Michigan
cases.FraudEntity: Leticia Gallarzo (posed as licensed registered nurse; nursing home unit manager)
cases.State_County: Michigan - Western District of Michigan (formerly of Wayland, Michigan)
cases.SchemeSummary: Gallarzo created a fake nursing license, diploma and identification documents and assumed the identity of a real Michigan-licensed registered nurse to obtain employment at a nursing home through Indeed.com, where she performed patient assessments, administered medications, started IV lines and was promoted to unit manager supervising other clinicians; after pleading guilty she fled and again fraudulently obtained work as a physician assistant and RN in Illinois and California.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
cases.FraudEntity: Trang Pharmacy (Worcester-based pharmacy)
cases.SchemeSummary: Trang Pharmacy submitted Medicare Part D claims for dispensing medications it could not prove it had ever purchased, i.e., it lacked the inventory to have dispensed the drugs billed to beneficiaries; it agreed to pay $750,000 to resolve the False Claims Act allegations.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of North Carolina
cases.FraudEntity: Kathy Briggs (co-owner); Neveah & Company d/b/a Restorative Medical
cases.State_County: North Carolina - Forsyth County (Winston-Salem); North Carolina - Yadkin County (Yadkinville)
cases.SchemeSummary: Briggs's durable medical equipment company, which supplied incontinence products to about 50 assisted living facilities, billed Medicaid each month for the maximum reimbursable quantity of adult diapers per beneficiary (e.g., 200) regardless of how many were actually delivered, since employees only restocked shelves to that level; Medicaid paid about $2.4 million for undelivered product.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Illinois
cases.FraudEntity: Shawn Bashir (created fictitious therapy companies); Clarence W. Brown III (Chicago chiropractor); Walgreens (pharmacy chain); 13 unnamed defendants charged in the Northern District of Illinois as part of the national health care fraud takedown
cases.PayerName: Medicare; HHS Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA); unnamed private insurers
cases.SchemeSummary: Year-in-review summary of the district's healthcare fraud docket: 13 defendants charged in the national takedown allegedly billed over $1.83 billion to HRSA, Medicare and private insurers (over $865 million paid); Shawn Bashir allegedly set up fictitious therapy companies to submit more than $17.3 million in false claims to a private insurer; chiropractor Clarence W. Brown III billed a private insurer over $2 million for nonexistent services and was sentenced to nearly six years; and Walgreens agreed to pay up to $350 million to resolve False Claims Act allegations that it filled invalid opioid prescriptions and billed Medicare and other federal programs for them.  Figures span multiple defendants.

cases.JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Rhode Island
cases.FraudEntity: Zynex, Inc. (Colorado-based medical device company); Thomas Sandgaard (former CEO); Anna Lucsok (former Chief Operating Officer)
cases.PayerName: TRICARE; other government health care payors (VA, federal employee programs); private health insurers; patients
cases.SchemeSummary: Zynex admitted, in a non-prosecution agreement, to submitting excessive and improper claims to TRICARE, other government and private payors, and patients for electrotherapy devices and supplies, shipping and billing for medically unnecessary quantities of supplies (as many as 32, 64 or 128 electrode pairs per patient per month), collecting more than $873 million (including over $600 million for supplies) largely through fraudulent billing, and concealing from investors that revenue was driven by that billing; the company will pay $5-$12.5 million and forfeit unpaid claims including over $85 million billed to TRICARE during a payment suspension and over $13 million billed to other payors/patients, while its former CEO and COO were separately indicted.
